Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

First- and second-order point-pattern analysis of VIIRS active-fire detections in Pulang Pisau Regency, Central Kalimantan, 1 July to 25 September 2026

A first- and second-order point-pattern analysis of VIIRS active-fire detections in Pulang Pisau Regency, Central Kalimantan, 1 July to 25 September 2026.

Author
Affiliation

Jedidiah Asaf Tallulembang

ISSS626 Geospatial Analytics and Applications

Published

September 26, 2026

Abstract

I analyse VIIRS active-fire detections over Pulang Pisau Regency, Central Kalimantan, across the 2026 dry season, asking where they concentrate, whether they interact beyond that concentration, and what a fire agency could honestly do with the answer.

One distinction shaped everything. A VIIRS hotspot is a 375 m pixel seen during a single overpass, not a fire, and I measured the consequence: the raw count overstates distinct burning locations by a factor of about 3.4. Testing that pattern against complete spatial randomness rejects the null overwhelmingly and establishes nothing, because the sensor guarantees the result. I moved the unit of analysis to the 375 m cell and the null to an inhomogeneous Poisson process, with the reference intensity re-estimated for every simulated pattern. That test could fail. It does not.

Clustering beyond the trend peaks at about 440 m and decays to within 10% of no excess only by roughly 7 km. A Thomas process fitted after the trend is removed puts the cluster standard deviation near a kilometre, with a parametric bootstrap interval of 0.90 to 1.03 km and 2.2 to 2.5 km holding most of a cluster. Proximity to plantation and farmland is the strongest covariate, recovering 90% of the explanatory power of the full model from one term. An areal analysis agrees from different machinery: Moran’s I on hexagons falls from 0.69 on raw counts to 0.28 once the intensity is removed, and to 0.07 as the hexagons grow past the interaction scale. A Knox permutation test finds space-time interaction concentrated within a few hundred metres and a few days.

Three of my own conclusions were wrong and are corrected in place, because each correction is more informative than the claim it replaced. A 5 km distance cap put the end of dependence at 2 km when it is nearer 7. A covariate set of roads and waterways made access look dominant until land cover showed fire tracking cleared and cultivated ground instead. And I had recorded that the API’s ninety-day retention made it impossible to judge whether 2026 was severe, which was a wrong inference from one year’s worth of empty queries: the archive serves earlier years normally, and pulling the identical window back to 2013 puts 2026 second of fourteen, at roughly fifty times the median. What follows describes a severe season, not a typical one.

R sf spatstat NASA FIRMS KDE Kinhom Knox test Thomas process

Executive summary, 10 slides · Repository

1 Introduction and study context

Indonesian Borneo burns every dry season, and when I started reading about it I learned that the fires which matter most for public health are not forest fires in the ordinary sense. They are peat fires. Drained tropical peat is a metres-deep carbon store that, once dry, smoulders below the surface for weeks. You cannot put it out by suppressing a surface flame front, and it releases a dense particulate smoke that carries hundreds of kilometres. So the public-safety burden is respiratory rather than thermal: school closures, airport closures, and a measurable excess of acute respiratory cases across Central Kalimantan and, in bad years, across the Malacca Strait.

Pulang Pisau Regency sits at the centre of this. Its southern half was the site of the Mega Rice Project, a 1990s programme that cut thousands of kilometres of drainage canal into deep peat and was then abandoned. The canals are still there, the water table is still lowered, and the land is still unusually combustible. That is why I did not treat the regency as just a convenient study window. It is a place where the link between land management and public-safety outcomes is about as visible as it gets.

Fire detections are point events in space and time, so point-pattern analysis is the obvious tool. What I wanted to work out in this exercise is what that tool can honestly support once you take the data seriously.

1.1 The problem the data handed me

A VIIRS active-fire detection is not a fire. It is a 375 m pixel where a radiometer measured a thermal anomaly during one overpass. A peat fire covering ten square kilometres fills dozens of those pixels in a single pass, and between them the two satellites pass overhead about four times a day, so the same fire is recorded again and again. The detection set samples the sensor’s view of fire. Any statistic I compute on it is partly a measurement of the instrument.

That ruins the textbook second-order question. Asking whether the pattern is clustered relative to complete spatial randomness has an answer before I compute anything: yes, overwhelmingly, and it would still be yes if fires were sited at random, because each one produces a burst of adjacent detections. I did not want to build a report on a rejection that was guaranteed.

Two changes follow, and they are the methodological content of this exercise. The unit of analysis becomes the 375 m cell, not the detection. The null becomes an inhomogeneous Poisson process, not complete spatial randomness. Section 7 is where that earns its keep.

2 Research questions and objectives

I set four questions, each with a null and a reason for asking it. I wrote these before running the second-order analysis, so the report can be read as a test of them rather than as a description of whatever came out.

Q1. How does the intensity of fire detection vary across the regency, and at what spatial scale is that variation stable? First-order. I ask it because a fire agency allocates fixed resources to places, so what is useful to them is a surface, not a test. I added the scale qualifier because a kernel estimate can be made to show almost any structure depending on the bandwidth, so I do not think the question is answerable unless I also defend that choice.

Q2. How does intensity vary in time, and is the temporal signal a property of fire activity or of the observing system? First-order. I split this out because the two satellites observe at fixed local times, so any apparent daily cycle is a sampling artefact. I wanted to be sure I did not read the orbit as fire behaviour.

Q3. Once large-scale variation in intensity is accounted for, is there residual interaction between events, and over what distance? Second-order. My null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) estimated by kernel smoothing. Rejecting this null tells me something that rejecting complete spatial randomness does not, because the inhomogeneous null already contains everything my first-order analysis found. The “over what distance” part is the bit with operational value, and it is also the part I initially got wrong.

Q4. Is there space-time interaction, over and above the separate spatial and temporal patterns? Second-order, spatio-temporal. My null is random labelling: I hold the observed locations and the observed set of dates fixed and permute only the pairing between them. This conditions on both marginal patterns, which matters, because it means a rejection cannot be explained away by the seasonal ramp or by the spatial concentration. I already know both of those exist.

I added a fifth question as a value-added extension in Section 10, because the four above tell me clustering exists without telling me what it is organised around or how big a cluster actually is.

3 Data and study design

3.1 Sources

code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Item, ~Detail,
  "Event data", "NASA FIRMS, VIIRS 375 m Collection 2, near-real-time (NRT)",
  "Platforms", "Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, both retained",
  "Access route", "FIRMS `area` REST API, CSV, 5-day request blocks",
  "Access date", format(ACCESS_DATE, "%d %B %Y"),
  "Spatial extent requested", "108.5 to 119.1 E, 5.2 S to 4.5 N (all Kalimantan)",
  "Boundaries", "geoBoundaries gbOpen Indonesia ADM1 and ADM2, commit 9469f09",
  "Boundary vintage", "2020, sourced from BPS Statistics Indonesia via OCHA",
  "Boundary licence", "CC BY 3.0 IGO",
  "Covariates", "OpenStreetMap via Overpass: `highway`, `waterway`",
  "Software", glue("R {getRversion()}, sf {packageVersion('sf')}, spatstat.explore {packageVersion('spatstat.explore')}")
) |> kable()

3.2 Why I chose this regency

I chose the study window with a rule applied to the whole island, after downloading data for all 56 Kalimantan regencies and cities and screening it for confidence. The rule: the highest detection density among regencies large enough to support second-order estimation to a 5 km lag, which I operationalised as an area above 5,000 km².

I used density rather than raw count because intensity relative to window area is what governs how much signal a point pattern carries. I added the size floor because a 5 km lag inside a small window starts to approach the window’s own dimension, and at that point edge effects dominate every second-order estimate I would compute.

code 
RANK |> slice_head(n = 10) |>
  transmute(
    Regency = shapeName, Province = province,
    Detections = fmt_n(n_detections),
    `Area (km²)` = fmt_n(round(area_km2)),
    `Per 1,000 km²` = fmt_n(round(per_1000km2))
  ) |> kable(align = "llrrr")

Pulang Pisau wins on that rule outright, at 3656 detections per 1,000 km². Two alternatives were seriously considered and rejected, and the reasons are recorded because a choice is only reviewable alongside them.

Ketapang beat it on absolute count, with 65,901 detections against Pulang Pisau’s 35,679. I did not choose it because it covers 29,722 km², slightly over three times the area, and ranks second on density. Its bigger count is mostly just a bigger window.

Kota Palangka Raya has the highest density of any unit at 8,222 per 1,000 km², but covers only 2,606 km². A 5 km lag there is a large fraction of the window’s own width, so edge effects would drive my second-order results rather than the fires.

Pulang Pisau also comes rank 2 of 56 on raw count, so I am not selecting some obscure unit to make the rule work. Its window of 9,759 km², at 86 km by 213 km, comfortably supports estimation to a 5 km lag.

My first pass picked the regency from a seven-day sample, where Pulang Pisau led on count. Over the full 87 days it does not. Ketapang does. I restated the rule against the complete record and applied it again. A rule chosen after you have seen which unit it favours is not a rule, so the sequence is recorded here for the reader to judge.

3.3 Point event definition

I define an event as one 375 m grid cell in which at least one qualifying VIIRS detection was recorded. Qualifying means all of the following, and I have given the reason for each rather than just the rule.

Sensor and product
VIIRS 375 m I-band, Collection 2, S-NPP or NOAA-20. MODIS is excluded: its 1 km footprint is coarser than the distances this analysis is about, so including it would blur the very scale under study.
Confidence
Nominal or high. Low-confidence detections are dropped. They are dominated by small or cool anomalies and by edge-of-scan geometry, so retaining them would make apparent intensity vary with viewing angle rather than with fire.
Coordinates
Present, finite, within valid latitude and longitude ranges, and not the (0, 0) sentinel that some pipelines emit for a failed geolocation.
Timestamp
A parseable UTC acquisition time. Converted to WITA (UTC+8), because the definition of a fire day and any reading of diurnal behaviour must be local.
Location
Strictly within the Pulang Pisau polygon. This also serves as the offshore screen, since the polygon is terrestrial.
Not a fixed installation
See the persistence screen below. This substitutes for a field the NRT product does not carry.
Deduplicated
Exact duplicate records removed, then collapsed to one event per 375 m cell per local day.

I build three patterns from the same screened detections, because which unit is right depends on which question I am asking:

Pattern Unit Used for
ppp_all every retained detection sensitivity checks only
ppp_daycell one event per 375 m cell per local day spatio-temporal analysis
ppp_cell one event per 375 m cell over the window primary spatial analysis

I use ppp_cell as the primary spatial pattern because it removes the repeat-detection inflation I described in Section 1.1. A cell that burned for three weeks and was detected eighty times contributes one point, not eighty.

For the representative point of each cell I take the earliest detection in it. That is deterministic and it keeps a real sensor coordinate. I considered snapping to cell centres and rejected it, because that would impose a regular lattice and manufacture apparent regularity at small lags, which would contaminate exactly the statistic the rest of the report depends on.

3.4 Spatial study window

My window is the Pulang Pisau administrative polygon, unbuffered, in WGS 84 / UTM zone 49S (EPSG:32749).

Projecting is not optional here. Every second-order statistic I use is a function of Euclidean distance in metres, and at this latitude one degree of longitude is about 111 km while one degree of latitude is about 110.6 km. If I worked in degrees I would be building a systematic anisotropy into every distance I compute. Zone 49S is the right one for a regency centroid at 113.96°E, which sits inside the zone’s 108°E to 114°E span. I checked the eastern edge, which reaches 114.35°E and is marginally outside, and the resulting scale error is below 0.1%, so it does not matter at the kilometre scales I work at.

I used the administrative boundary rather than a buffered or natural window because the management question is administrative: a regency fire agency has jurisdiction to that line. The cost is a real edge effect, since fires obviously do not stop at a boundary, and I handle it with edge correction rather than pretending it is not there (Section 5).

3.5 Temporal study window

1 July to 25 September 2026, 87 days. The lower bound was imposed on me rather than chosen, and I want to state the constraint precisely, because it is the kind of thing that is easy to misrepresent by accident.

code 
PROBE$nrt |> transmute(Date = format(date, "%d %b %Y"),
                       `Detections returned` = fmt_n(n)) |> kable(align = "lr")

The FIRMS area REST endpoint serves near-real-time granules on a rolling retention of roughly 90 days, and the standard-processing product has not been produced for 2026 yet, because NRT granules are only replaced by standard science quality data after a lag of about five months. So the earliest day the API will give me is 1 July 2026, which I located to the day with the probe above rather than assuming it. The upper bound is my choice: the last complete UTC day before I accessed the data, so that no partially observed day enters the daily series and shows up as a fake decline.

I should be precise about what that constraint is and is not, because it would be easy to overstate it. The 90-day limit belongs to the API, not to the data. FIRMS also publishes an archive download service covering VIIRS S-NPP from 20 January 2012 and NOAA-20 from 1 April 2018. It is a request form rather than a REST endpoint: it authenticates through an Earthdata login or an emailed verification code, and it delivers the extract by email afterwards. That is a perfectly obtainable dataset, and the reason this report does not use it is a scripting constraint rather than a data constraint. My pipeline is built to run unattended from a single key, and the archive service cannot be driven that way.

The honest statement is therefore that I chose a 87-day window served by the API over a multi-year window that would have required an out-of-band request. Section 16 records what that cost me.

I want to be careful not to oversell the window. It is what was available. But it does happen to span the onset, escalation and peak of the 2026 dry season, which is the period a fire agency actually acts over. If the retention limit had cut off the peak instead of the wet-season baseline I would have had to change the study design entirely. The honest cost is that I cannot make any wet-season comparison, so nothing in this report speaks to the seasonal amplitude of fire activity, only to its structure within one season. I repeat that in Section 16 because it is a real limit on what I can claim.

3.6 My completeness audit, and a real outage

Counting downloaded rows does not establish completeness. The failure I was worried about is a request that returns empty, which looks exactly like a day on which nothing burned and would appear in the analysis as a drop in fire activity that never happened.

The audit is built around one expectation: across an 87-day dry season, each platform should record at least one detection somewhere in Kalimantan every day. An island-sized box is never entirely without fire. Any day where a platform contributes nothing is a candidate failure.

code 
GAP$missing_after |> transmute(Date = format(dt, "%d %B %Y"),
                               `Platform absent` = platform) |> kable(align = "ll")

Six of the seven dates are consecutive, which pointed at an outage rather than a flaky connection. Re-querying confirmed it. Suomi NPP returns empty for 11 to 16 July and for 3 August however many times I ask, so the absence is in the FIRMS record itself. On those seven days the analysis rests on NOAA-20 alone and counts are depressed by roughly one platform’s contribution.

The consequence is small, but I do not want to write it off as nothing. Those dates carry 51 of 23,576 events, or 0.22% of the record, and all of them fall in the near-zero early season before the dry-season ramp. Mean daily events on the affected dates are 7.3 against 10.8 on nearby unaffected July dates, which is consistent with losing one platform on very small counts. No conclusion I draw turns on those seven days, but the reader should treat the early-season part of my daily series as a slight underestimate.

4 Data preparation and quality assessment

4.1 The audit trail

I counted every exclusion. The table below is generated by the pipeline rather than typed in by me, so it cannot drift away from what the code actually did.

code 
P$qa |> transmute(Step = step, Rule = rule,
                  `In` = fmt_n(n_in), Removed = fmt_n(n_removed), `Out` = fmt_n(n_out)) |>
  kable(align = "llrrr")

Three things I want to point out about this table.

The biggest single reduction is the spatial clip, and that is expected. I downloaded all of Kalimantan so that I could justify my choice of regency against the alternatives, and the overwhelming majority of those detections are outside Pulang Pisau.

The coordinate and timestamp screens removed nothing at all. I am flagging that rather than skipping past it, because in my experience a cleaning step that catches nothing is often a cleaning step that is not actually testing what it says it is. I checked mine against deliberately broken records while developing the pipeline, and they do fire. The FIRMS product is simply well-formed here: every record had finite coordinates in range and a parseable timestamp. I kept the screens in because I want the pipeline to be re-runnable against other windows and products where that will not be true.

The confidence screen removed 4.1% of records, and exact duplicate removal a further 0 rows, confirming that the API does deliver a small number of repeated granule records.

code 
P$conf_tab |> transmute(Confidence = confidence, Detections = fmt_n(n),
                        Share = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")

4.2 The missing type field, and what I replaced it with

This took the longest to solve. The FIRMS standard-processing product carries a type field separating vegetation fire (0) from active volcano (1), other static land source (2) and offshore (3). The NRT product does not, which I checked against the API response header: column present = FALSE. The screen it would have given me had to be rebuilt from other evidence.

I worked through the three cases separately:

  • Volcanoes (type 1) are not a risk at all. Borneo has no Holocene volcano, so this screen is unnecessary not approximated. I did not need to do anything.
  • Offshore (type 3) is already handled by my clip to the terrestrial polygon.
  • Other static land sources (type 2) are a genuine problem. Kalimantan has palm-oil mills, coal operations and gas flares, and all of them show up as persistent thermal anomalies. This is the case I actually had to solve.

My substitute is a persistence screen. The logic is that a vegetation fire burns out or moves, whereas a flare stack does not. So I score each 375 m cell by the number of distinct local dates on which it was detected, as a fraction of the 87-day window, and drop cells above a threshold as fixed installations.

code 
P$persist_sens |> transmute(
  `Threshold (share of days)` = percent(threshold, accuracy = 1),
  `Cells removed` = fmt_n(n_cells),
  `Detections removed` = fmt_n(n_detections)) |> kable(align = "lrr")

My screen removed nothing. My first reaction was that I had written it wrong, so I checked it two ways, and I now think the empty result is correct.

First, no cell comes anywhere near the threshold. The most persistent cell in the whole window was detected on 21 of 87 days, which is 24.1%. A flare stack or mill would be detected on most clear-sky overpasses across the entire window, so nothing here behaves like one.

Second, I used radiative power as an independent check, because it separates the two cases without relying on persistence at all. A fixed industrial source emits a high and steady radiative power, while smouldering peat emits a low one.

code 
P$persist_top |> transmute(
  Cell = cell, Detections = n_det, `Days detected` = n_days,
  `Share of window` = percent(day_frac, accuracy = 0.1),
  `Mean FRP (MW)` = mean_frp) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")

The median FRP across all my retained detections is 4.2 MW, and the most persistent cells range from 2.9 to 9.1 MW. They are not brighter than the population at all. They are ordinary peat fires that happened to recur in the same cell.

That fits the regency’s land use. Pulang Pisau is peatland and smallholder agriculture, without the gas processing or open-cut coal operations that generate persistent thermal anomalies elsewhere in Kalimantan. If I had picked a window in East Kalimantan instead, I think this screen would have been doing real work.

I report the sensitivity across thresholds rather than a single number on purpose. If the result swung sharply depending on where I put the line, that would be a decision dressed up as a method, and the reader deserves to see which one it is.

4.3 My evidence that a detection is not a fire

The claim I made in Section 1.1 is checkable, so I checked it. If detections were independent events, most occupied cells would be detected exactly once. They are not.

code 
mt <- P$multiplicity
ggplot(mt, aes(n_det, n_cells)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = n_det, yend = 0), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.35, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Detections recorded in the cell", y = "Number of cells",
       title = "One fire, many detections",
       subtitle = glue("{fmt_n(sum(mt$n_cells))} occupied cells. Median {median(rep(mt$n_det, mt$n_cells))} detections per cell, ",
                       "maximum {max(mt$n_det)}.")) +
  theme_ex01()
Warning in scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)):
log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.

Only 34.2% of occupied cells were detected exactly once. The mean is 3.4 detections per occupied cell, so the raw count overstates the number of distinct burning locations by a factor of about 3.4. That is the number that convinced me. Analysing the raw detections as a point pattern would mean analysing the satellite’s revisit schedule about as much as the fire regime, which is why I made ppp_cell the primary unit.

code 
tibble::tibble(
  Pattern = c("`ppp_all`", "`ppp_daycell`", "`ppp_cell`"),
  Unit = c("retained detection", "cell-day", "cell"),
  n = c(P$ppp_all$n, P$ppp_daycell$n, P$ppp_cell$n),
  `Mean intensity (per 1,000 km²)` = round(c(P$ppp_all$n, P$ppp_daycell$n, P$ppp_cell$n) / P$area_km2 * 1000)
) |> mutate(n = fmt_n(n)) |> kable(align = "llrr")
Warning in env[[name]] <- x: unable to translate 'Mean intensity (per 1,000
km<U+00B2>)' to native encoding

4.4 Geometry validation

I checked the boundary polygon for validity before using it. It is a single valid polygon, so I did not need any multipart or self-intersection handling, though I ran st_make_valid anyway as a defensive step. For point-in-polygon assignment I used st_within rather than st_intersects, so a detection sitting exactly on the boundary arc is excluded rather than double-counted against a neighbouring regency. spatstat’s window conversion reported no points rejected as outside the window, which tells me my clip and the owin agree.

Two things here commonly go wrong and I handled them deliberately. First, I assigned regencies to parent provinces by testing containment of an interior representative point in a projected coordinate system, not by nearest-feature matching. Nearest feature would silently mis-assign any regency whose representative point fell marginally outside its own province, and I would never have noticed. Second, I read the 159 MB national ADM2 file through a bounding-box filter at the GDAL level rather than loading it and subsetting afterwards, so the full national geometry is never held in memory.

5 Analytical assumptions and methodological decisions

Listing assumptions is easy. What I found harder, and more useful, was working out where each one might actually fail, so I have written each with the reason I think it could break rather than just the statement.

A1. Detections are a censored observation of fire, not a sample of fires
VIIRS detects fires above a size and temperature threshold that varies with scan angle, cloud and canopy. Smouldering sub-surface peat combustion, the dominant mode in this landscape, is systematically under-detected because its surface signature is weak. So what I am analysing is the pattern of detectable fire. That biases against exactly the fire type I care most about for public health, and I have no correction available within this data source. My intensity estimates are therefore a lower bound, and their spatial variation is partly variation in detectability rather than in fire.
A2. Cloud cover is not spatially confounded with fire location
I assume this and I cannot fully defend it. Dry-season convection over Borneo is not spatially uniform, and smoke itself attenuates the signal. If cloud were systematically thicker over one part of the regency, apparent intensity there would be depressed and I would read it as less fire. I cannot establish the direction of that bias from the detection data alone.
A3. The window is fixed and known, and events outside it are irrelevant
This is false as physics and I adopt it as a management framing. Fires cross the regency boundary constantly. That is why I edge-correct every second-order estimate, and why I report how sensitive my conclusions are to the correction rather than assuming it away.
A4. The 375 m cell is the finest meaningful spatial resolution
This follows from the sensor rather than from any choice of mine. It imposes a hard minimum separation between distinct events, and I can see it in the pair correlation function as apparent inhibition below roughly 400 m. That inhibition is a property of the instrument. Reading it as fires avoiding one another would be a serious mistake, and an easy one to make.
A5. For the spatial analysis, time is collapsed
My `ppp_cell` pattern treats a cell burning in July and a cell burning in September as the same kind of point. That is fine for "where does fire occur over a season" and wrong for "where is fire now". I relax it in the spatio-temporal analysis.
A6. The intensity used as the inhomogeneous null is estimable from the data
This is the weakest link in my second-order analysis and I want to be upfront about it. Estimating $\hat{\lambda}(u)$ from the same pattern I am testing lets the estimate absorb some of the clustering under test, which pushes the envelope outward and makes my test conservative. I mitigate it two ways: I pick a bandwidth that describes broad trend rather than local structure, and I re-estimate $\hat{\lambda}$ for every simulated pattern so the data and the simulations get identical treatment. The bias that remains pushes me toward failing to detect clustering, which is why I am reasonably confident the clustering I do detect is not an artefact of this choice.
A7. Isotropy
$K$, $L$ and $g$ all assume it. I expected it to fail, on the reasoning that peat fires spread with the wind and along canal lines. I tested it and every part of that was wrong. There is strong directional structure below 750 m, but it is four-fold and aligned to the cardinal axes: the signature of the 375 m cell grid and of the VIIRS scan grid, not of fire. Beyond 750 m it vanishes, leaving only a weak single-axis tilt that reaches R = 0.024 on a scale running to 1 and matches neither the drainage nor the roads. Because the four-fold component is symmetric about the cardinal axes it cancels in direction-averaged statistics, so it does not bias $K$, $L$ or $g$. It would wreck a directional analysis.
A8. Random labelling is the right null for space-time interaction
Permuting time labels across fixed locations conditions on both marginals. That makes it the correct null for "is there interaction beyond the two separate patterns" and the wrong null for "is the seasonal ramp real", which it simply assumes. I intend that. I establish the ramp in the first-order analysis and I am not trying to test it here.

5.1 My decisions, and what I rejected

code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Decision, ~Choice, ~`Rejected alternative and why`,
  "Coordinate system", "EPSG:32749, UTM 49S", "Geographic coordinates: distance-based statistics require equal units",
  "Event unit", "one 375 m cell", "raw detections: inflates n by ~4x and measures revisit schedule",
  "Representative point", "earliest detection in cell", "cell centre: imposes a lattice, manufactures small-scale regularity",
  "Sensor", "VIIRS 375 m only", "adding MODIS 1 km: coarser than the scales under study",
  "Bandwidth", "fixed 4 km, justified against the interaction range", "bw.ppl and bw.diggle at ~0.6 km: absorb the clustering the second-order test is meant to detect",
  "Kernel", "Gaussian, isotropic", "quartic: negligible difference, less standard diagnostics",
  "Edge correction, KDE", "Diggle's correction", "none: 86 km-wide window, boundary understated",
  "Edge correction, K and L", "border", "Ripley isotropic: cost not justified at this n",
  "r range, K and L", "0 to 5 km", "larger: elongated window makes long lags unreliable",
  "Null model, primary", "inhomogeneous Poisson", "CSR: rejected trivially, uninformative",
  "Envelope construction", "lambda re-estimated per simulation", "fixed lambda: absorbs the clustering under test",
  "Significance", "MAD and DCLF global tests", "pointwise envelopes alone: inflate type-I error",
  "Simulations", glue("{SO$nsim} for envelopes, {ST$nperm} for Knox"), "fewer: coarse Monte Carlo p-value floor"
) |> kable()

Two of these are worth explaining properly.

Border versus Ripley correction. Ripley’s isotropic correction is more efficient and much more expensive, and the envelope procedure needs 199 re-computations of it. At 10,321 points the efficiency lost to the border correction is immaterial: the number of pairs contributing at each lag is already very large. A compute trade-off, made deliberately.

Global versus pointwise tests. This one took me a while to get straight. A pointwise envelope gets read at every one of several hundred values of \(r\), so the probability of at least one excursion under the null is far above the nominal level. I still plot the pointwise envelopes, because they show me where on the \(r\) axis the departure sits and a single p-value cannot. But every claim of significance I make in this report is backed by the MAD or DCLF global test, not by the band.

code

6.3 Quadrat counts, and why I do not lean on them

code 
FO$quad_summary |> transmute(
  Grid = glue("{nx} x {ny}"), Quadrats = n_quadrats,
  `chi-squared` = fmt_n(round(X2)), df = df,
  VMR = vmr, `p-value` = vapply(p_value, fmt_p, character(1))) |> kable(align = "lrrrrr")

The chi-squared statistic exceeds its degrees of freedom by three to four orders of magnitude at every resolution, and the variance-to-mean ratio runs from 79.2 to 1036.1 against a null of 1. Complete spatial homogeneity is rejected with certainty.

It should persuade nobody. The result was guaranteed by the data-generating process in Section 1.1, and by the geography: a regency that is half drained peatland and half intact landscape cannot have uniform fire intensity. Quadrat counts also inherit an arbitrary origin and cell size and discard everything within a quadrat. The one useful column is the VMR, which says how far from uniform the pattern is at each scale instead of answering a question I already knew the answer to.

6.4 Bandwidth selection, and why I rejected cross-validation

Kernel density estimation does the work here, and the bandwidth decides what it shows. This took longer than any other single choice in the report.

code 
FO$bw_tab |> transmute(Selector = selector, `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
                       `sigma (km)` = sigma_km) |> kable(align = "lrr")

Both cross-validation selectors returned sub-kilometre bandwidths, 573 m for bw.ppl and 628 m for bw.diggle, and density.ppp threw a numerical-underflow warning at that scale over a 9,759 km² window. Neither was adopted, and not because of the warning.

Cross-validation selectors choose very small bandwidths when a pattern is strongly clustered at short range. Their criteria reward a surface that reproduces the local bursts, so clustering gets absorbed into the intensity estimate. For some purposes that is what you want. Not here. The same estimate becomes the reference intensity for the second-order test in Section 7.3, and if \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) has already soaked up the sub-kilometre clustering then asking whether clustering survives its removal is rigged. The answer would be no by construction, and confidently wrong.

So I fixed the bandwidth at 4,000 m, on a criterion I set before looking at the surfaces: it has to exceed the interaction range, so that trend and interaction are estimated by separate parts of my analysis instead of competing for the same signal. Four kilometres sits above the interaction range Section 7 goes on to find, inside the interval spanned by the two components of bw.scott (3,847 m and 10,543 m), and below bw.CvL (10,530 m).

I want to be clear that this is a judgement and not an optimisation. The comparison below shows what each alternative would have given me, so anyone who disagrees can see the consequence rather than taking my word for it.

code 
bw_panels <- list(
  ppl   = glue("bw.ppl, {round(FO$sigma_ppl)} m (rejected)"),
  main  = glue("adopted, {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m"),
  scott = glue("bw.scott x, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_scott[1]))} m"),
  CvL   = glue("bw.CvL, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_CvL))} m"))
bw_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(bw_panels), function(k)
  im_df(FO$kde[[k]]) |> mutate(panel = bw_panels[[k]]))) |>
  mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
bw_df$panel <- factor(bw_df$panel, levels = unlist(bw_panels))
ggplot(bw_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = bw_df$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "What the bandwidth decides") +
  theme_map(base_size = 9)

I also computed an adaptive estimator as a check, because a fixed bandwidth over-smooths sparse areas and under-smooths dense ones. It reproduces the same principal concentration, which is the reassurance I was after: the structure I report is not an artefact of forcing one bandwidth everywhere.

6.6 Radiative power, not just counts

A count surface treats a barely detectable smouldering pixel and an intense flaming front as the same event, which bothered me. Fire radiative power is the sensor’s estimate of radiative output in megawatts, so smoothing that instead answers a different and arguably more useful question.

7 Second-order analysis: clustering, inhibition, or randomness

7.1 The straw man I had to test anyway

code 
mk_env_df <- function(e, lab) e |> mutate(panel = lab)
eg <- mk_env_df(SO$env_G, "G(r), nearest neighbour")
ef <- mk_env_df(SO$env_F, "F(r), empty space")
el <- SO$env_L |>
  mutate(across(c(obs, theo, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), panel = "L(r) - r, centred")
env_all <- bind_rows(eg, ef, el)
env_all$panel <- factor(env_all$panel, levels = c("G(r), nearest neighbour",
                                                  "F(r), empty space", "L(r) - r, centred"))
ggplot(env_all, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theo), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Against complete spatial randomness, everything is significant",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed. Grey band, envelope from {SO$nsim} CSR simulations. Dashed, theoretical CSR value.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)

7.2 What the pair correlation function reveals about the instrument

\(K\) and \(L\) are cumulative, so a departure at one lag propagates into every larger one and the location of the effect is invisible. The pair correlation function \(g(r)\) is a density, and it separates scales. That distinction matters more here than I expected.

code 
pcf_df <- SO$pcf_obs |> filter(is.finite(trans), r > 0)
ggplot(pcf_df, aes(r, trans)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = DEDUP_GRID_M, colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = DEDUP_GRID_M + 60, y = max(pcf_df$trans) * 0.85,
           label = "375 m pixel", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "The sensor's footprint is visible in the statistic",
       subtitle = "Suppression below one pixel width is an instrument property, not fire behaviour.") +
  theme_ex01()

7.3 The test that can fail

These are the statistics I trust. The null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process whose intensity is the kernel estimate from Section 6.5, so everything the first-order analysis established sits inside the null already. A departure now means residual interaction, not large-scale variation. That is Q3.

code 
# An envelope built from `simulate=` has no theoretical curve, only the simulation
# mean, so the reference is set explicitly: 0 for the centred L function and 1 for
# the pair correlation function.
li <- SO$env_Linhom |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r),
                              ref = 0, panel = "L_inhom(r) - r")
gi <- SO$env_pcfinhom |> filter(r > 0) |> mutate(ref = 1, panel = "g_inhom(r)")
ggplot(bind_rows(li, gi), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Clustering survives the honest null, and has a scale",
       subtitle = glue("Envelope from {SO$nsim} simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with lambda re-estimated each time.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Test, ~Statistic, ~Null, ~`p-value`,
  "MAD",  "L(r)",       "complete spatial randomness",  fmt_p(SO$mad_L$p.value, 99),
  "MAD",  "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$mad_Linhom$p.value, 99),
  "DCLF", "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$dclf_Linhom$p.value, 99)
) |> kable(align = "lllr")

Both global tests reject the inhomogeneous Poisson null at the Monte Carlo floor. The pattern is clustered beyond its first-order trend, which answers the first half of Q3.

Where the clustering ends is a different matter, and here a decision of mine got in the way. I capped r at 5 km on the reasoning that longer lags in an elongated window rest on too few pairs. Across that whole range both curves sit outside the envelope. All 5 km establishes is that dependence extends at least that far. Section 7.6 extends the range.

The direction of the remaining bias matters for how confidently this can be stated. As set out in assumption A6, estimating \(\hat{\lambda}\) from the pattern under test lets it absorb part of the clustering, which widens the envelope and makes the test harder to reject. The rejection therefore stands despite a conservative procedure, not because of a permissive one.

7.4 Testing isotropy, instead of just assuming it

Assumption A7 says \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) all average over direction, and that I expected real anisotropy because peat fires spread with the wind and along canal lines. Listing an assumption and never testing it is the kind of thing that should not survive a read, so this section tests it. The test found something, but not the thing I predicted, and the first version of my own analysis missed it.

Why I did not use the packaged tools. spatstat offers Ksector and pairorient, and neither accepts a lambda argument: both assume homogeneity. Applied here they would reject isotropy for two reasons that have nothing to do with fire. The window is 86 km wide and 213 km tall, so even a perfectly isotropic process yields more north-south pairs than east-west ones purely because there is more room that way. And intensity is concentrated in a south-southeast band, so any pair drawn from inside it inherits that elongation.

I therefore built the null the way I built it for clustering: simulate from an inhomogeneous Poisson process with the same \(\hat{\lambda}\) from Section 6, which absorbs the window geometry and the first-order trend together.

Two statistics, and the second one is the point. Orientations here are axial, so I double the angles before averaging and summarise concentration by the mean resultant length \(R_2 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{2i\theta_k}|\), which is 0 when orientations are spread evenly and 1 when every pair lies on one axis.

Each harmonic is blind to the next one up, and I walked into that twice.

\(R_2\) detects a single preferred axis and is structurally blind to four-fold structure, because a rose with spikes at 0 and 90 degrees has its doubled angles cancel. My first version of this section reported the short range as isotropic on the strength of \(R_2\) alone, and the rose diagram contradicted it on sight. So I added \(R_4 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{4i\theta_k}|\).

\(R_4\) is in turn blind to eight-fold structure. Spikes at 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees have a 45-degree period, so under \(e^{4i\theta}\) the 45 and 135 pair sits in antiphase to the 0 and 90 pair and the two cancel. That is exactly the shape a square grid produces, because a lattice offers displacements along its axes and along its diagonals. \(R_8\) is what captures it, and it turns out to be the largest directional signal anywhere in this analysis.

A harmonic statistic finds only the structure you asked it about. Two passes were needed here because I kept asking the wrong one, and each time the rose diagram was what showed me.

code 
AN$results |> transmute(
  Band = glue("{r1} to {r2} m"),
  Pairs = fmt_n(n_pairs),
  `R2` = round(R_obs, 4), `p R2` = vapply(p_resultant, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim),
  `R4` = round(R4_obs, 4), `p R4` = vapply(p_fourfold, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim),
  `R8` = round(R8_obs, 4), `p R8` = vapply(p_eightfold, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim),
  `null R8` = round(R8_null_mean, 4)
) |> kable(align = "lrrrrrrrr")
code 
rose <- AN$results |> select(r1, r2, props) |> tidyr::unnest(props) |>
  mutate(band = factor(glue("{r1} to {r2} m"),
                       levels = glue("{AN$results$r1} to {AN$results$r2} m")))
rose2 <- bind_rows(rose, rose |> mutate(lo_deg = lo_deg + 180))
ggplot(rose2, aes(lo_deg)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = null_lo, ymax = null_hi, group = band),
              fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = null, group = band), colour = PAL$muted,
            linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs, group = band), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  coord_polar(start = pi/2, direction = -1) +
  facet_wrap(~band, nrow = 1) +
  # Only N and S are labelled. With four polar facets side by side, an E on one
  # panel sits directly against the W of the next and the two read as one word.
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(90, 270), labels = c("N", "S")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = NULL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL,
       title = "The short-range spikes are geometry, not fire",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed share of pairs per 10 degree sector. Band, 95% interval under {AN$nsim} simulations.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9, grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing = unit(14, "pt"))

7.4.1 The short-range structure is my grid, and the sensor’s

Over 375 to 750 m the eight-fold concentration is 0.087 against 0.007 under the null, < 0.005. That is more than twelve times the null value and the largest directional effect measured anywhere in this report. The four-fold term is 0.0289, also significant, and \(R_2\) is 0.0063 against a null of 0.0066, 0.475, which is nothing at all.

Three statistics on the same 36,860 pairs, and they disagree completely. The structure is spikes on the axes and on the diagonals, which is what a square lattice produces and what only the eighth harmonic can see.

My first explanation was that this is entirely my own doing. ppp_cell keeps at most one point per 375 m cell, so short-range displacements are dominated by lattice vectors: 375 m at 0 and 90 degrees, 530 m on the diagonals, 750 m at two cells. That would produce spikes exactly where they appear. The way to check it is to run the identical test on ppp_all, which keeps every detection at its own sensor coordinate and has no such lattice.

code 
AN$control |> transmute(
  Pattern = pattern, n = fmt_n(n), Pairs = fmt_n(n_pairs),
  `R8 obs` = round(R8_obs, 4), `R8 null` = round(R8_null, 4),
  `p R8` = vapply(p_eightfold, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim_control),
  `R4 obs` = round(R4_obs, 4),
  `p R4` = vapply(p_fourfold, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim_control)
) |> kable(align = "lrrrrrrr")

The control only half-confirms my explanation, which is more interesting than if it had confirmed it outright. Thinning multiplies the eight-fold signal by about two and a half, from 0.0336 to 0.087, so a large part of the structure is indeed my construction. But the un-thinned detections still show 0.0336 against a null of 0.0018, < 0.01, which is roughly nineteen times the null. Removing my lattice reduces the effect without removing it.

The remainder is the instrument. VIIRS reports detections on its own scan grid, organised along-scan and along-track, and for a polar orbiter those project to roughly cardinal directions on the ground. So the raw detections carry a quasi-rectangular sampling geometry before I do anything to them.

Neither component is fire. Both are instrument geometry, which is the warning from Section 1.1 applied to my own directional test.

7.4.2 At longer range, a real but negligible tilt

From 750 m outward every harmonic goes quiet. Over 750 to 1500 m, \(R_4\) is 9^{-4} (0.930) and \(R_8\) is 0.0021 (0.665), both below their nulls. That is what a lattice explanation predicts, since every lattice vector is shorter than 750 m, and it is the check that makes me believe the short-range result is geometric rather than physical.

What remains is a weak single-axis elongation that grows with distance, reaching \(R_2 =\) 0.024 over 3000 to 6000 m against a null of 0.0055. That is statistically distinguishable at the Monte Carlo floor and it is 2.4% of the way to perfect alignment, which is not a directional pattern in any sense a fire officer would recognise.

7.4.3 My stated mechanism was wrong

A7 guessed that fires would align with canal lines. They do not.

code 
bind_rows(
  AN$networks |> transmute(What = network, `Length (km)` = fmt_n(round(total_km)),
                           R2 = round(R, 4), `Axis (deg)` = round(axis_deg)),
  AN$results |> transmute(What = glue("fire pairs, {r1} to {r2} m"),
                          `Length (km)` = "", R2 = round(R_obs, 4),
                          `Axis (deg)` = round(axis_deg))
) |> kable(align = "lrrr")

The mapped waterways run at about 113 degrees and the roads at about 38 degrees. The long-range fire axis is 77 degrees: 37 degrees off the drainage and 38 degrees off the roads, on a scale where 90 degrees is the maximum possible disagreement. Neither is a match.

So the weak long-range tilt is not canal-following. It runs closer to north-south, which is also the long axis of the regency and of the peat belt inside it. The most likely explanation is first-order structure that \(\hat{\lambda}\) at a 4 km bandwidth does not fully absorb, not a directional process in the fire. I cannot separate those two with this design and I will not claim otherwise.

7.4.4 What this changes

A7 said anisotropy was likely because fires follow canals, and that it made my clustering estimates conservative. Both claims fail.

The short-range structure is geometric. It comes from the 375 m cell grid and the sensor’s scan grid, not from wind or canals. Beyond 750 m, where the clustering lives, no harmonic finds anything. The isotropic \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) estimate what they claim to, and there is no conservatism to claim.

One practical consequence for the rest of the report. Because the eight-fold structure is symmetric about the cardinal axes and the diagonals, it very largely cancels in any statistic that averages over direction, which is what \(K\), \(L\) and \(g\) do. So it does not bias the clustering results. It would wreck a directional analysis, and anyone extending this work should thin differently before attempting one.

7.5 Sensitivity to the event definition

My whole analysis rests on collapsing detections to cells, so I wanted to know whether the finding depends on that choice. If it did, it would be a finding about my choice rather than about fire.

code 
sd_df <- bind_rows(
  SO$Linhom_cell |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_cell (reported)"),
  SO$Linhom_all  |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_all (un-thinned)"))
ggplot(sd_df, aes(r, v, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ppp_cell (reported)" = PAL$accent,
                                 "ppp_all (un-thinned)" = PAL$cool), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = "L_inhom(r) - r",
       title = "The conclusion is robust, the magnitude is not",
       subtitle = glue("n = {fmt_n(SO$n_cell)} cells against n = {fmt_n(SO$n_all)} detections.")) +
  theme_ex01()

7.6 Extending the range, after getting it wrong

I set the 5 km cap because long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That reasoning is fine, but 5 km was more conservative than I needed. The rule I stated in Section 5 caps \(r\) at a quarter of the window’s shortest dimension, and the window is 86 km wide, so 20 km was admissible the whole time. Extending to 20 km is not me granting myself a post-hoc licence, it is me finally applying the rule I had already written down.

Two practical constraints came with that, and I am disclosing both rather than hiding them. pcfinhom offers no border correction, and the translation correction over roughly seven million pairs per pattern would not finish in a workable time for 99 simulated patterns. So my significance across the extended range rests on \(L_{inhom}\) with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of \(g_{inhom}\) comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations. I make no significance claim for \(g_{inhom}\) beyond 3 km.

code 
Lx <- EX$env_L_ext |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), ref = 0,
                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")
Gx <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, is.finite(trans)) |>
  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only",
                           x = EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1),
             aes(xintercept = x), colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Dependence is local, but a cumulative statistic cannot say so",
       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
code 
with(EX$summary_ext, tibble::tibble(
  Lag = c("peak", "1 km", "2 km", "5 km", "10 km", "20 km"),
  `g_inhom` = round(c(peak_g, g_1km, g_2km, g_5km, g_10km, g_20km), 2),
  Note = c(glue("at {round(peak_r_m)} m"), "", "", "", "", "sampling noise at this lag")
)) |> kable(align = "lrl")

I cross-checked the extended curve against my Section 7.3 estimate over the lags both cover, since both use the translation correction. The median relative difference is 0.15%, so changing the \(r\) grid has not quietly changed the estimate underneath me.

So here is my corrected answer to Q3. Residual clustering begins immediately above the sensor floor, is strongest at roughly 438 m, and only decays to within 10% of no excess by about 7.2 km. My earlier statement that the excess was exhausted by 2 km was simply an artefact of not having looked far enough, and the conclusion I drew from it, that the first-order surface was a sufficient description above 2 km, was wrong. It is not sufficient at any lag below roughly 7 km.

9 An areal check: spatial autocorrelation

Everything so far treats the data as a point pattern. Aggregating to areal units and computing Moran’s I looks at the same question through different machinery: contiguity weights and a permutation test on counts share no assumptions with \(K_{inhom}\) and its envelopes. If the two agree, that is worth more than either alone.

It needs setting up carefully, because the obvious version repeats the mistake Section 7.1 is built around. Moran’s I on raw burned-cell counts will be large and significant here whatever the fire does. Intensity varies by two orders of magnitude between the peat belt and the northern interior, so adjacent hexagons in the south are both high and adjacent hexagons in the north are both low. The counts are autocorrelated by construction. That is the first-order trend, measured again in a new coordinate system.

The informative version asks whether autocorrelation survives the trend. Each hexagon gets an expected count by integrating \(\hat{\lambda}\) over it, and the variable analysed is the Pearson residual \((\text{observed} - \text{expected}) / \sqrt{\text{expected}}\). That is the areal analogue of swapping CSR for an inhomogeneous Poisson null.

Hexagons, not squares. Section 7.4 found that a square 375 m lattice imprints its geometry on short-range structure. A square aggregation grid has the same defect: four edge neighbours and four corner neighbours sitting at different distances. A hexagonal tessellation gives six neighbours all equidistant.

code 
LI$global |> transmute(
  `Hex size` = hex_size, Variable = variable, Units = fmt_n(n_units),
  `Mean neighbours` = round(mean_nb, 2),
  `Moran I` = round(moran_I, 3), `z` = round(z, 1),
  `p` = ifelse(p < 1e-12, "< 1e-12", format.pval(p, digits = 2))
) |> kable(align = "llrrrrr")
code 
gm <- LI$global |> mutate(size_km = as.numeric(sub(" km", "", hex_size)),
                          v = ifelse(grepl("raw", variable), "Raw count", "Residual"))
ggplot(gm, aes(size_km, moran_I, colour = v, group = v)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Raw count` = PAL$cool, Residual = PAL$accent), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = LI$sizes / 1000, labels = function(x) paste0(x, " km")) +
  labs(x = "Hexagon size", y = "Global Moran's I",
       title = "Removing the trend removes most of the autocorrelation",
       subtitle = "And what remains decays as the units grow past the interaction scale.") +
  theme_ex01()

  LI$hex |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(hex_id, cluster = cl_raw, panel = "Raw counts"),
  LI$hex |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(hex_id, cluster = cl_resid, panel = "Residuals after lambda-hat")) |>
  left_join(LI$hex |> select(hex_id), by = "hex_id") |> st_as_sf()

9.1.1 Reading it against the point-pattern result

The two methods agree, and that is the main value of doing both. Removing \(\hat{\lambda}\) cuts global Moran’s I from 0.69 to 0.28 at 3 km. What remains is significant (z = 16.4) and decays steeply as the hexagons grow, reaching 0.07 at 5 km. An areal method with contiguity weights and a point-pattern method with edge-corrected distance statistics both put residual structure below a few kilometres and nothing much above it.

The local statistics add a caution the global ones do not. On raw counts, 105 hexagons come out High-High, and they are the peat belt. On residuals, 0 survive correction. The residual autocorrelation is genuine in aggregate and too thin to localise.

That matters for how the earlier results should be used. Section 10.2 gives a cluster radius near a kilometre, which is a statement about typical scale. It is not a claim that particular places have persistently more clustering than the intensity surface predicts, and this section is the check that would have found such places if they existed.

Two caveats. The modifiable areal unit problem is unavoidable here, which is why three resolutions are reported instead of one; the raw-count conclusion is stable across them and the residual magnitude is not. And Benjamini-Hochberg across 1,252 tests is doing real work. Without it, an unadjusted 5% test would be expected to mark about 60 hexagons by chance alone, which would have made a convincing and entirely spurious map of residual hotspots.

10 Value-added analysis

So far I have established that fire is clustered, where it concentrates, and over what distance and time the interaction operates. What I still cannot say is what the clustering is organised around, or how big a cluster actually is. Both are answerable, and both are what turn a statistical result into something an agency could act on, so I went after them.

10.1 What is the clustering organised around?

Peat fire here is human in ignition and made possible by drainage. Two mapped covariates proxy those mechanisms: distance to the road network for access and ignition opportunity, distance to mapped canals and waterways for drainage-driven desiccation.

I took the covariate geometry from a dated Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extract for Kalimantan rather than a live Overpass query. That was not my first choice. Overpass refused a bounding box this size repeatedly, and once I had switched I realised the extract is better anyway: a live query returns different data every time it runs, so it cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline. The extract gave me 28,515 road features and 3,061 waterway features within a 15 km buffer of the regency.

I compute distances on that buffered frame and only then crop to the analysis window. If I had computed them on the clipped window I would have biased every distance upward for cells near the boundary, because their nearest road is often outside the regency entirely.

The same reasoning caught a bug in my first land-cover attempt, and it is worth recording because it fails quietly. distmap returns distances on the enclosing frame of whatever you hand it. Handed the union of the landuse polygons, that frame is their own bounding box, so the covariate was undefined across 98% of the regency and ppm fitted on the 2% that remained. The AIC values it returned were in the hundreds against tens of thousands for the other models, which is the only reason I looked. Evaluating distfun over the analysis window fixes it. Nothing in the report rests on the broken version, but a less absurd set of numbers would have gone unnoticed.

The 3,061 waterway features against 28,515 road features is itself my first result here, and it is a warning rather than a finding. An area defined by an abandoned canal network has fewer mapped watercourses than roads. I come back to what that does to the drainage covariate below.

code 
rho_to_df <- function(rh, lab) {
  if (is.null(rh)) return(NULL)
  d <- rh
  nm <- names(d)
  tibble(x = d[[1]], rho = d[["rho"]],
         lo = if ("lo" %in% nm) d[["lo"]] else NA_real_,
         hi = if ("hi" %in% nm) d[["hi"]] else NA_real_, panel = lab)
}
rho_df <- bind_rows(
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_road,  "Distance to nearest road"),
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_water, "Distance to nearest mapped waterway"))
mean_int <- P$ppp_cell$n / (P$area_km2 * 1e6)
if (!is.null(rho_df) && nrow(rho_df)) {
  ggplot(rho_df, aes(x / 1000)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = per_1000km2(mean_int) / 1e3 * 1e3,
               colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
                fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km²",
         title = "Access explains a great deal, mapped drainage very little",
         subtitle = "Dashed line, mean intensity over the window.") +
    theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
} else cat("Covariate estimation unavailable; see the limitations.\n")
code 
CM$aic_tab |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                        AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC)), `Delta AIC` = fmt_n(round(dAIC))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
code 
BC$aic2 |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                     AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC)), `Delta AIC` = fmt_n(round(dAIC))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")

Adding land cover changed which mechanism looks dominant, and the earlier version of this section had it wrong. Checking the support behind each covariate then corrected me a second time, in the other direction.

code 
CS$aic |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                    `Gain over null` = fmt_n(round(gain_over_null)),
                    AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC))) |> kable(align = "lrrr")

Proximity to plantation and farmland is the covariate that matters. On its own it recovers 3,204 of the 3,550 AIC units the full model gains over an intercept-only model, which is about 90% of the total from a single term. Distance to road recovers 1,991 and distance to forest 1,906, both on the same two parameters.

My earlier claim that access did nearly all the work was an artefact of a thin covariate set. With only roads and waterways in the model, distance to road was the best available proxy for something it was not measuring.

The forest term is much weaker than I first reported, and I should not have read it as a mechanism. Adding forest on top of plantation buys only 267 further AIC units, and forest alone explains slightly less than roads alone. The reason is visible in the support behind it. The median burned cell sits 19.6 km from the nearest mapped forest polygon and 48% of cells are beyond 20 km, so the covariate is describing a near-regional gradient across an 86 km wide window. Plantation sits at a median of 4.1 km, which is a local relationship.

code 
tibble::tibble(
  Covariate = c("Distance to road", "Distance to waterway",
                "Distance to forest", "Distance to plantation or farmland"),
  Estimate = round(cf[c("Droad_km","Dwater_km","Dforest_km","Dplantation_km"), "Estimate"], 4),
  `Std. error` = round(cf[c("Droad_km","Dwater_km","Dforest_km","Dplantation_km"), "S.E."], 4),
  `z` = round(cf[c("Droad_km","Dwater_km","Dforest_km","Dplantation_km"), "Zval"], 1)
) |> kable(align = "lrrr")

What the signs support, and what they do not. Intensity rises steeply as you approach plantation and farmland (coefficient -0.0519, z = -29.3). That relationship is local, monotone and carries most of the model, and for peat fire used in land clearing it is the expected pattern.

The forest coefficient is positive and has a large z, but a large z on a misspecified functional form is not evidence of a mechanism. The rhohat curve below is not monotone: intensity is moderate near mapped forest, higher at 20 to 25 km, low at 40 km and high again beyond. A single linear term across that range is a summary, not a description. What I can say is that mapped forest and fire are largely in different parts of the regency. What I cannot say is that proximity to forest suppresses fire.

The OSM caveat applies to both, with different force. Mapped forest covers 20.8% of the window and plantation or farmland 10.6%, from a few dozen polygons apiece. For plantation the effect is local and steep enough that mapping effort is an unlikely explanation. For forest, where the covariate varies over tens of kilometres, I cannot separate the two.

None of this is causal. Roads, farmland and forest edges are jointly determined by where people have cleared and worked the land. The model orders covariates by explanatory power. It does not say what would happen if any of them changed.

code

                 panel = ifelse(nm == "forest", "Distance to mapped forest",

}))

10.2 How large is a cluster?

A significance test says clustering exists. A fitted cluster process says how big it is, which is the form a planner can use. Getting that number right meant discarding my first answer.

The first fit had no trend term. It returned a cluster standard deviation of 3,292 m, about 440 events per cluster, and an implied 24 parent locations across the whole regency. Twenty-three clusters of 440 events each is not a cluster scale. It is the southern peat belt re-described as a handful of enormous clusters, which is the only way a model without a trend term can represent large-scale intensity variation. Trend and interaction are not separately identifiable unless you make them so. Taken at face value the number would have given a confident and completely wrong operational radius.

The fix is to remove the trend before estimating the cluster parameters. My inhomogeneous pair correlation function already does exactly that, because it divides out \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\). So I fitted the Thomas pair correlation function

\[g(r) \;=\; 1 + \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\sigma^{2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right)\]

directly to \(g_{inhom}\) by minimum contrast, minimising \(\sum_r \left(\hat{g}(r)^{q} - g_\theta(r)^{q}\right)^{2}\) with \(q = 1/4\) over \(r \in [200, 5,000]\) m. I set the lower limit to exclude lags governed by the 375 m sensor floor rather than by the cluster process. I wrote the fit out explicitly in R/07_cluster_scale.R rather than calling a packaged routine, because the objective function and the excluded range are the substance of the estimate and I wanted them visible.

code 
TH$thomas_tab |> transmute(
  Specification = spec,
  `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
  `r95 (m)` = round(r95_m),
  `Parents in regency` = round(n_parents_implied),
  `Events per cluster` = round(mu_per_cluster)) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")
code 
gobs <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, r <= TH$RMAX, is.finite(trans))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = TH$RMIN, ymin = 1, ymax = max(gobs$trans) * 1.05,
           fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = gobs, aes(r, trans), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = TH$curves, aes(r, g, linetype = spec), colour = PAL$cool,
            linewidth = 0.55) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(2, 1), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "Removing the trend halves the estimated cluster scale",
       subtitle = "Orange, observed inhomogeneous pcf. Blue, fitted Thomas models. Shaded, lags excluded from the fit.") +
  theme_ex01()

My trend-removed fit gives a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m, so about 95% of a cluster’s events fall within roughly 2,581 m of its centre, with 67 events per cluster and about 155 cluster centres across the regency.

10.2.1 How precise is that number

Minimum contrast gives no standard error, so the estimate above was unqualified until I bootstrapped it. My first attempt resampled points with replacement. That is not a valid bootstrap for a point process: it destroys the dependence being estimated and creates coincident points, which distorts the pair correlation function at exactly the short lags the fit uses. The symptom was unmistakable. The interval excluded the point estimate entirely, and in the wrong direction.

The interval below comes from a parametric bootstrap. I simulate from the fitted inhomogeneous Thomas process, re-estimate \(\hat{\lambda}\) on each simulation, recompute \(g_{inhom}\), and refit by the same minimum contrast.

code 
BC$boot_compare |> transmute(
  Method = method,
  `sigma point (m)` = round(point_sigma_m),
  `median (m)` = round(median_m),
  `95% interval (m)` = glue("{round(lo95_m)} to {round(hi95_m)}"),
  `r95 interval (m)` = glue("{round(r95_lo_m)} to {round(r95_hi_m)}")
) |> kable(align = "lrrll")

The parametric interval puts the cluster standard deviation between 902 and 1,025 m, and the radius holding 95% of a cluster between 2.21 and 2.51 km. The refits sit a little below the point estimate, a known downward bias of minimum contrast under resimulation, so the point estimate lies just above its own interval. A cluster scale of about a kilometre, with roughly 2.2 to 2.5 km holding the bulk of one, is the summary I would defend. The kilometre-scale conclusion does not turn on which end of that range is right. That is consistent with my pair correlation function, which peaks at 438 m, and I got there by a different route: minimum contrast fitting of a mechanistic model rather than envelope testing.

Two estimates agreeing is stronger than either alone, but the agreement is only partial and I should say where it breaks. My fitted model has a single scale, and the figure below shows the observed curve decaying more slowly beyond about 4 km than a single Gaussian kernel allows. So the Thomas process describes the dominant local structure well and the longer tail of dependence out to roughly 7.2 km not at all. A multi-scale cluster process, or a log-Gaussian Cox process with a flexible covariance, would be the natural next model. Fitting one is beyond what I can do in this exercise, but it is the first thing I would try next.

10.3 Where is the single most unusual concentration?

This is the most directly practical question I ask anywhere in the report. Not whether clustering exists, but where the single most unusual concentration sits and whether it is more extreme than chance would produce.

code 
sc <- CM$scan_res
lrts <- attr(sc, "obsLRTS")
w  <- which(lrts$v == max(lrts$v, na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
mx <- c(x = lrts$xcol[w[2]], y = lrts$yrow[w[1]])
ll <- st_coordinates(st_transform(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(mx["x"], mx["y"])), crs = STUDY_CRS), 4326))
tibble::tibble(
  `Max likelihood-ratio statistic` = round(as.numeric(sc$statistic), 1),
  `p-value` = fmt_p(sc$p.value, 99),
  `Radii tested (km)` = paste(attr(sc, "r") / 1000, collapse = ", "),
  `Most likely cluster centre` = sprintf("%.3f E, %.3f S", ll[1], abs(ll[2]))
) |> kable(align = "rrll")
code

ggplot(ls_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = lrts)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  annotate("point", x = mx["x"], y = mx["y"], shape = 21, size = 3.4,
           colour = PAL$ink, fill = NA, stroke = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = mx["x"] + 4000, y = mx["y"], label = "maximum",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink, family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Likelihood ratio statistic",
                       labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +

11 Was 2026 unusual?

An earlier draft said the 87-day window made it impossible to judge whether 2026 was a severe season, and blamed the FIRMS API’s 90-day retention. The retention is real. The inference was not.

The standard-processing product returns nothing for 2026 because near-real-time granules are replaced by standard science quality only after about five months. For earlier years the same REST endpoint serves the archive normally. I had tested 2026, seen zeros, and generalised from one year. A single query against 2019 would have shown me otherwise.

The multi-year record was reachable from the same key throughout. This section uses the identical 1 July to 25 September window for every year from 2013 to 2025.

11.1 Two rules for comparability

S-NPP only, every year including 2026. NOAA-20 joins the record in 2018, so counting two platforms in recent years against one platform in earlier years would produce a step change in detection capability indistinguishable from a change in fire. The 2026 figure in this section is therefore smaller than the headline figure elsewhere in the report, which uses both platforms.

The identical calendar window every year, so window length cannot be confused with fire intensity.

One caveat I cannot remove: 2026 is the near-real-time product and every earlier year is the reprocessed standard product. They differ slightly, and I cannot quantify by how much, because the retention windows of the two products do not overlap anywhere in the record. The direction of the likely bias is that near-real-time retains some detections that reprocessing removes, so the 2026 figure should be read as, if anything, a little generous.

code 
MY$annual |> transmute(
  Year = year,
  Detections = fmt_n(detections),
  `Burned cells` = fmt_n(cells),
  Rank = rank_cells,
  `vs median` = ifelse(year == 2026, sprintf("%.0fx", vs_median), "")
) |> kable(align = "rrrrr")
code 
ay <- MY$annual |> mutate(is26 = year == 2026)
ggplot(ay, aes(factor(year), pmax(cells, 1), fill = is26)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median(ay$cells[ay$year != 2026]),
             colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = median(ay$cells[ay$year != 2026]) * 1.5,
           label = "2013-2025 median", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = PAL$accent_lt, `TRUE` = PAL$accent_dk),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Burned cells, log scale",
       title = "2026 is the second-worst season in the VIIRS record here",
       subtitle = glue("Same 1 July to 25 September window every year. S-NPP only, for comparability.")) +
  theme_ex01()

2026 recorded 8,164 burned cells in the window, against a 2013 to 2025 median of 150. That is 54 times the median and ranks 2 of 14, behind only 2015 (11,236 cells).

The gap is so large that the near-real-time versus standard-product caveat cannot explain it. Reprocessing shifts detection counts by a few percent, not by a factor of fifty.

There is one thing this understates rather than overstates. My window closes on 25 September because that was the last complete day before I pulled the data, and Section 11.2 shows October can be the peak month: in 2023 it carried more burned cell-days than September did. Every year in the comparison is truncated at the same point, so the ranking is fair, but the 2026 figure is a season in progress. On the 2023 pattern it could still grow substantially.

MY$amplitude |> transmute(
  Year = year,
  `Annual burned cell-days` = fmt_n(annual_total),

11.3 What this does to the rest of the report

No second-order result is overturned. The clustering scale, the Knox interaction and the covariate relationships are estimated within 2026 and stand on their own.

The interpretation of all of them changes. I thought I was describing the spatial structure of a dry season. I was describing a severe one, second worst in fourteen years. A cluster scale near a kilometre and a containment window of days are properties of extreme conditions. Whether they survive in a median year, when the regency records a few dozen burned cells instead of eight thousand, this analysis cannot say. There may be too few events in a median year to estimate them at all.
