# Second-order analysis: clustering, inhibition, or randomness {#sec-second-order}

## The straw man I had to test anyway {#sec-strawman}

```{r fig-csr}
#| label: fig-csr
#| fig-cap: "Nearest-neighbour G, empty-space F, and the centred L function, each against a complete spatial randomness envelope from 199 simulations. What I take from it: every statistic departs from the CSR envelope immediately and by an enormous margin. G rises far faster than expected, meaning nearest neighbours are much closer than random; F rises far slower, meaning empty gaps are much larger than random; L sits far above zero at every lag. Read naively this is overwhelming evidence of clustering. Read correctly it is evidence of almost nothing, because the sensor guarantees this result: a single fire produces adjacent detections. I include it to make that failure visible rather than hide it. The analysis I actually rely on is in Section 7.3."
#| fig-height: 3.4
mk_env_df <- function(e, lab) e |> mutate(panel = lab)
eg <- mk_env_df(SO$env_G, "G(r), nearest neighbour")
ef <- mk_env_df(SO$env_F, "F(r), empty space")
el <- SO$env_L |>
  mutate(across(c(obs, theo, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), panel = "L(r) - r, centred")
env_all <- bind_rows(eg, ef, el)
env_all$panel <- factor(env_all$panel, levels = c("G(r), nearest neighbour",
                                                  "F(r), empty space", "L(r) - r, centred"))
ggplot(env_all, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theo), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Against complete spatial randomness, everything is significant",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed. Grey band, envelope from {SO$nsim} CSR simulations. Dashed, theoretical CSR value.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

## What the pair correlation function reveals about the instrument

$K$ and $L$ are cumulative, so a departure at one lag propagates into every larger
one and the location of the effect is invisible. The pair correlation function
$g(r)$ is a density, and it separates scales. That distinction matters more here
than I expected.

```{r fig-pcf}
#| label: fig-pcf
#| fig-cap: "Pair correlation function of the primary pattern, log scale. The dotted line marks the 375 m VIIRS pixel dimension. What I take from it: g(r) is suppressed at very short range and peaks at about 460 m, immediately above the pixel width. This is not fires avoiding one another. It is the sensor's resolution: two detections cannot be much closer than one pixel, because one pixel yields one detection. That short-range suppression is an instrument artefact and is the clearest single piece of evidence that this pattern records observation rather than events. Above the peak, g(r) decays slowly and is still above 3 at 2.9 km, nowhere near its asymptote of 1. So spatial dependence extends well beyond the 5 km range I plot here, which is what pushed me to the extended range in Section 7.6."
#| fig-height: 3.6
pcf_df <- SO$pcf_obs |> filter(is.finite(trans), r > 0)
ggplot(pcf_df, aes(r, trans)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = DEDUP_GRID_M, colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = DEDUP_GRID_M + 60, y = max(pcf_df$trans) * 0.85,
           label = "375 m pixel", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "The sensor's footprint is visible in the statistic",
       subtitle = "Suppression below one pixel width is an instrument property, not fire behaviour.") +
  theme_ex01()
```

## The test that can fail {#sec-honest-test}

These are the statistics I trust. The null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process
whose intensity is the kernel estimate from @sec-intensity, so everything the
first-order analysis established sits inside the null already. A departure now means
residual interaction, not large-scale variation. That is Q3.

```{r fig-inhom}
#| label: fig-inhom
#| fig-cap: "Inhomogeneous centred L function and inhomogeneous pair correlation function, against envelopes from 199 simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process. The reference intensity is re-estimated for every simulated pattern. What I take from it: the departure survives, and it does not close. Both curves leave the envelope at about 100 m and remain outside it across the entire range plotted. g_inhom peaks near 5.9 at roughly 570 m and is still above 2 at 2.8 km, against an envelope ceiling near 1.4. So after accounting for the fact that fire is far more likely in the southern peat belt than in the north, burned cells still occur much closer together than that variation alone predicts. Note also that g_inhom falls below 1 at the shortest lags, the sensor floor surviving into the inhomogeneous statistic."
#| fig-height: 3.6
# An envelope built from `simulate=` has no theoretical curve, only the simulation
# mean, so the reference is set explicitly: 0 for the centred L function and 1 for
# the pair correlation function.
li <- SO$env_Linhom |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r),
                              ref = 0, panel = "L_inhom(r) - r")
gi <- SO$env_pcfinhom |> filter(r > 0) |> mutate(ref = 1, panel = "g_inhom(r)")
ggplot(bind_rows(li, gi), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Clustering survives the honest null, and has a scale",
       subtitle = glue("Envelope from {SO$nsim} simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with lambda re-estimated each time.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

```{r tbl-global}
#| label: tbl-global
#| tbl-cap: "Global Monte Carlo tests. The maximum absolute deviation (MAD) and Diggle-Cressie-Loosmore-Ford (DCLF) statistics each summarise the whole curve in one number, so these p-values are not inflated by reading a band at many lags. The Monte Carlo floor is 0.01 with 99 simulations."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Test, ~Statistic, ~Null, ~`p-value`,
  "MAD",  "L(r)",       "complete spatial randomness",  fmt_p(SO$mad_L$p.value, 99),
  "MAD",  "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$mad_Linhom$p.value, 99),
  "DCLF", "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$dclf_Linhom$p.value, 99)
) |> kable(align = "lllr")
```

Both global tests reject the inhomogeneous Poisson null at the Monte Carlo floor.
The pattern is clustered beyond its first-order trend, which answers the first half
of Q3.

Where the clustering ends is a different matter, and here a decision of mine got in
the way. I capped r at 5 km on the reasoning that longer lags in an elongated window
rest on too few pairs. Across that whole range both curves sit outside the envelope.
All 5 km establishes is that dependence extends *at least* that far. @sec-extended
extends the range.

The direction of the remaining bias matters for how confidently this can be
stated. As set out in assumption A6, estimating $\hat{\lambda}$ from the pattern
under test lets it absorb part of the clustering, which widens the envelope and
makes the test *harder* to reject. The rejection therefore stands despite a
conservative procedure, not because of a permissive one.

## Testing isotropy, instead of just assuming it {#sec-isotropy}

Assumption A7 says $K$, $L$ and $g$ all average over direction, and that I expected
real anisotropy because peat fires spread with the wind and along canal lines.
Listing an assumption and never testing it is the kind of thing that should not
survive a read, so this section tests it. The test found something, but not the
thing I predicted, and the first version of my own analysis missed it.

**Why I did not use the packaged tools.** `spatstat` offers `Ksector` and
`pairorient`, and neither accepts a `lambda` argument: both assume homogeneity.
Applied here they would reject isotropy for two reasons that have nothing to do
with fire. The window is 86 km wide and 213 km tall, so even a perfectly isotropic
process yields more north-south pairs than east-west ones purely because there is
more room that way. And intensity is concentrated in a south-southeast band, so any
pair drawn from inside it inherits that elongation.

I therefore built the null the way I built it for clustering: simulate from an
inhomogeneous Poisson process with the same $\hat{\lambda}$ from @sec-first-order, which
absorbs the window geometry and the first-order trend together.

**Two statistics, and the second one is the point.** Orientations here are axial, so
I double the angles before averaging and summarise concentration by the mean
resultant length $R_2 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{2i\theta_k}|$, which is 0 when
orientations are spread evenly and 1 when every pair lies on one axis.

Each harmonic is blind to the next one up, and I walked into that twice.

$R_2$ detects a single preferred axis and is **structurally blind to four-fold
structure**, because a rose with spikes at 0 and 90 degrees has its doubled angles
cancel. My first version of this section reported the short range as isotropic on
the strength of $R_2$ alone, and the rose diagram contradicted it on sight. So I
added $R_4 = |n^{-1}\sum_k e^{4i\theta_k}|$.

$R_4$ is in turn blind to **eight-fold** structure. Spikes at 0, 45, 90 and 135
degrees have a 45-degree period, so under $e^{4i\theta}$ the 45 and 135 pair sits
in antiphase to the 0 and 90 pair and the two cancel. That is exactly the shape a
square grid produces, because a lattice offers displacements along its axes *and*
along its diagonals. $R_8$ is what captures it, and it turns out to be the largest
directional signal anywhere in this analysis.

A harmonic statistic finds only the structure you asked it about. Two passes were
needed here because I kept asking the wrong one, and each time the rose diagram was
what showed me.

```{r tbl-aniso}
#| label: tbl-aniso
#| tbl-cap: "Directional structure by distance band against 199 simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process in the same window. R2 detects a single preferred axis, R4 four-fold structure, R8 eight-fold. Note that at 375 to 750 m the three disagree completely: R2 sees nothing, R4 sees something, and R8 sees the largest effect in the whole analysis."
AN$results |> transmute(
  Band = glue("{r1} to {r2} m"),
  Pairs = fmt_n(n_pairs),
  `R2` = round(R_obs, 4), `p R2` = vapply(p_resultant, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim),
  `R4` = round(R4_obs, 4), `p R4` = vapply(p_fourfold, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim),
  `R8` = round(R8_obs, 4), `p R8` = vapply(p_eightfold, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim),
  `null R8` = round(R8_null_mean, 4)
) |> kable(align = "lrrrrrrrr")
```

```{r fig-aniso}
#| label: fig-aniso
#| fig-cap: "Orientation of close pairs by distance band, as a rose diagram, against the 95% interval from 199 inhomogeneous Poisson simulations. Each rose is mirrored across the origin because orientations are axial. What I take from it: the shortest band is not isotropic at all. It has eight sharp spikes on the cardinal axes and the diagonals, which is the signature of a square grid rather than of fire, and my R2 statistic scored it as isotropic because R2 cannot see four-fold structure. The figure caught what the table missed. From 750 m outward the spikes vanish and the roses sit close to their null intervals, with only a slight and growing elongation by 3 to 6 km."
#| fig-height: 4.2
rose <- AN$results |> select(r1, r2, props) |> tidyr::unnest(props) |>
  mutate(band = factor(glue("{r1} to {r2} m"),
                       levels = glue("{AN$results$r1} to {AN$results$r2} m")))
rose2 <- bind_rows(rose, rose |> mutate(lo_deg = lo_deg + 180))
ggplot(rose2, aes(lo_deg)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = null_lo, ymax = null_hi, group = band),
              fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = null, group = band), colour = PAL$muted,
            linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs, group = band), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  coord_polar(start = pi/2, direction = -1) +
  facet_wrap(~band, nrow = 1) +
  # Only N and S are labelled. With four polar facets side by side, an E on one
  # panel sits directly against the W of the next and the two read as one word.
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(90, 270), labels = c("N", "S")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = NULL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL,
       title = "The short-range spikes are geometry, not fire",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed share of pairs per 10 degree sector. Band, 95% interval under {AN$nsim} simulations.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9, grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing = unit(14, "pt"))
```

```{r}
#| label: aniso-inline
#| include: false
a_short <- AN$results |> filter(r1 == 375)
a_mid   <- AN$results |> filter(r1 == 750)
a_long  <- AN$results |> filter(r1 == 3000)
wat <- AN$networks |> filter(network == "waterways")
rds <- AN$networks |> filter(network == "roads")
ctl_cell <- AN$control |> filter(grepl("ppp_cell", pattern))
ctl_all  <- AN$control |> filter(grepl("ppp_all", pattern))
axsep <- function(a, b) { d <- abs(a - b) %% 180; pmin(d, 180 - d) }
```

### The short-range structure is my grid, and the sensor's

Over `r a_short$r1` to `r a_short$r2` m the eight-fold concentration is
`r round(a_short$R8_obs, 4)` against `r round(a_short$R8_null_mean, 4)` under the
null, `r fmt_p(a_short$p_eightfold, AN$nsim)`. That is more than twelve times the
null value and the largest directional effect measured anywhere in this report. The
four-fold term is `r round(a_short$R4_obs, 4)`, also significant, and $R_2$ is
`r round(a_short$R_obs, 4)` against a null of `r round(a_short$R_null_mean, 4)`,
`r fmt_p(a_short$p_resultant, AN$nsim)`, which is nothing at all.

Three statistics on the same 36,860 pairs, and they disagree completely. The
structure is spikes on the axes and on the diagonals, which is what a square
lattice produces and what only the eighth harmonic can see.

My first explanation was that this is entirely my own doing. `ppp_cell` keeps at
most one point per 375 m cell, so short-range displacements are dominated by
lattice vectors: 375 m at 0 and 90 degrees, 530 m on the diagonals, 750 m at two
cells. That would produce spikes exactly where they appear. The way to check it is
to run the identical test on `ppp_all`, which keeps every detection at its own
sensor coordinate and has no such lattice.

```{r tbl-aniso-control}
#| label: tbl-aniso-control
#| tbl-cap: "The same test over 375 to 750 m, on the thinned pattern and on the un-thinned detections. If the spikes were purely an artefact of my cell thinning, the second row would show nothing. It does not."
AN$control |> transmute(
  Pattern = pattern, n = fmt_n(n), Pairs = fmt_n(n_pairs),
  `R8 obs` = round(R8_obs, 4), `R8 null` = round(R8_null, 4),
  `p R8` = vapply(p_eightfold, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim_control),
  `R4 obs` = round(R4_obs, 4),
  `p R4` = vapply(p_fourfold, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = AN$nsim_control)
) |> kable(align = "lrrrrrrr")
```

The control only half-confirms my explanation, which is more interesting than if it
had confirmed it outright. Thinning multiplies the eight-fold signal by about two
and a half, from `r round(ctl_all$R8_obs, 4)` to `r round(ctl_cell$R8_obs, 4)`, so
a large part of the structure is indeed my construction. But the un-thinned
detections still show `r round(ctl_all$R8_obs, 4)` against a null of
`r round(ctl_all$R8_null, 4)`, `r fmt_p(ctl_all$p_eightfold, AN$nsim_control)`,
which is roughly nineteen times the null. Removing my lattice reduces the effect
without removing it.

The remainder is the instrument. VIIRS reports detections on its own scan grid,
organised along-scan and along-track, and for a polar orbiter those project to
roughly cardinal directions on the ground. So the raw detections carry a
quasi-rectangular sampling geometry before I do anything to them.

Neither component is fire. Both are instrument geometry, which is the warning from @sec-not-a-fire applied to my own directional test.

### At longer range, a real but negligible tilt

From 750 m outward every harmonic goes quiet. Over
`r a_mid$r1` to `r a_mid$r2` m, $R_4$ is `r round(a_mid$R4_obs, 4)`
(`r fmt_p(a_mid$p_fourfold, AN$nsim)`) and $R_8$ is `r round(a_mid$R8_obs, 4)`
(`r fmt_p(a_mid$p_eightfold, AN$nsim)`), both below their nulls. That is what a
lattice explanation predicts, since every lattice vector is shorter than 750 m, and
it is the check that makes me believe the short-range result is geometric rather
than physical.

What remains is a weak single-axis elongation that grows with distance, reaching
$R_2 =$ `r round(a_long$R_obs, 4)` over `r a_long$r1` to `r a_long$r2` m against a
null of `r round(a_long$R_null_mean, 4)`. That is statistically distinguishable at
the Monte Carlo floor and it is 2.4% of the way to perfect alignment, which is not
a directional pattern in any sense a fire officer would recognise.

### My stated mechanism was wrong

A7 guessed that fires would align with canal lines. They do not.

```{r tbl-aniso-net}
#| label: tbl-aniso-net
#| tbl-cap: "Orientation of the mapped drainage and road networks inside the regency, weighted by segment length, against the fire pair-orientation axis at each band. Separation is axial, so 90 degrees is the maximum possible disagreement."
bind_rows(
  AN$networks |> transmute(What = network, `Length (km)` = fmt_n(round(total_km)),
                           R2 = round(R, 4), `Axis (deg)` = round(axis_deg)),
  AN$results |> transmute(What = glue("fire pairs, {r1} to {r2} m"),
                          `Length (km)` = "", R2 = round(R_obs, 4),
                          `Axis (deg)` = round(axis_deg))
) |> kable(align = "lrrr")
```

The mapped waterways run at about `r round(wat$axis_deg)` degrees and the roads at
about `r round(rds$axis_deg)` degrees. The long-range fire axis is
`r round(a_long$axis_deg)` degrees: `r round(axsep(a_long$axis_deg, wat$axis_deg))`
degrees off the drainage and `r round(axsep(a_long$axis_deg, rds$axis_deg))` degrees
off the roads, on a scale where 90 degrees is the maximum possible disagreement.
Neither is a match.

So the weak long-range tilt is not canal-following. It runs closer to north-south,
which is also the long axis of the regency and of the peat belt inside it. The most
likely explanation is first-order structure that $\hat{\lambda}$ at a 4 km
bandwidth does not fully absorb, not a directional process in the fire. I
cannot separate those two with this design and I will not claim otherwise.

### What this changes

A7 said anisotropy was likely because fires follow canals, and that it made my
clustering estimates conservative. Both claims fail.

The short-range structure is geometric. It comes from the 375 m cell grid and the
sensor's scan grid, not from wind or canals. Beyond 750 m, where the clustering
lives, no harmonic finds anything. The isotropic $K$, $L$ and $g$ estimate what they
claim to, and there is no conservatism to claim.

One practical consequence for the rest of the report. Because the eight-fold
structure is symmetric about the cardinal axes and the diagonals, it very largely
cancels in any statistic that averages over direction, which is what $K$, $L$ and
$g$ do. So it does not bias the clustering results. It would wreck a directional
analysis, and anyone extending this work should thin differently before attempting
one.

## Sensitivity to the event definition

My whole analysis rests on collapsing detections to cells, so I wanted to know
whether the finding depends on that choice. If it did, it would be a finding about
my choice rather than about fire.

```{r fig-sens}
#| label: fig-sens
#| fig-cap: "Inhomogeneous centred L function computed on the cell pattern and on the un-thinned detection pattern, on a common axis. What I take from it: both curves are positive, so the qualitative conclusion of residual clustering does not depend on the event definition. The magnitudes differ by roughly an order of magnitude, and the un-thinned pattern shows far stronger apparent clustering at every lag. That gap is the repeat-detection artefact measured directly. It is why I use the cell pattern for inference and the detection pattern only for this check. If I reported the upper curve I would be reporting the satellite revisit schedule as a fire-behaviour result."
#| fig-height: 3.4
sd_df <- bind_rows(
  SO$Linhom_cell |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_cell (reported)"),
  SO$Linhom_all  |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_all (un-thinned)"))
ggplot(sd_df, aes(r, v, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ppp_cell (reported)" = PAL$accent,
                                 "ppp_all (un-thinned)" = PAL$cool), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = "L_inhom(r) - r",
       title = "The conclusion is robust, the magnitude is not",
       subtitle = glue("n = {fmt_n(SO$n_cell)} cells against n = {fmt_n(SO$n_all)} detections.")) +
  theme_ex01()
```

## Extending the range, after getting it wrong {#sec-extended}

I set the 5 km cap because long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That
reasoning is fine, but 5 km was more conservative than I needed. The rule I stated in @sec-assumptions caps $r$ at a quarter of the window's shortest dimension, and the window is
`r round((bb["xmax"]-bb["xmin"])/1000)` km wide, so 20 km was admissible the whole
time. Extending to 20 km is not me granting myself a post-hoc licence, it is me
finally applying the rule I had already written down.

Two practical constraints came with that, and I am disclosing both rather than
hiding them. `pcfinhom` offers no border correction, and the translation correction
over roughly seven million pairs per pattern would not finish in a workable time for
99 simulated patterns. So my significance across the extended range rests on
$L_{inhom}$ with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of
$g_{inhom}$ comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations.
**I make no significance claim for $g_{inhom}$ beyond 3 km.**

```{r fig-ext}
#| label: fig-ext
#| fig-cap: "Left, inhomogeneous centred L function to 20 km with a 99-simulation envelope. Right, the observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function over the same range, with no envelope, on a log scale. What I take from it: the two panels answer different questions and disagree in an instructive way. g_inhom, which localises scale, peaks at about 440 m and decays steadily: it is 4.3 at 1 km, 2.7 at 2 km, 1.4 at 5 km, and reaches within 10% of its asymptote of 1 at about 7.2 km. L_inhom, which is cumulative, never re-enters its envelope within 20 km. Both are correct. The excess pair density is a local phenomenon that has largely dissipated by 7 km, and because L accumulates every excess at smaller lags it remains significantly elevated far beyond the range over which anything is actually happening."
#| fig-height: 3.6
Lx <- EX$env_L_ext |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), ref = 0,
                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")
Gx <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, is.finite(trans)) |>
  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only",
                           x = EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1),
             aes(xintercept = x), colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Dependence is local, but a cumulative statistic cannot say so",
       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

```{r tbl-ext}
#| label: tbl-ext
#| tbl-cap: "Observed inhomogeneous pair correlation at selected lags. A value of 1 means no excess over the inhomogeneous Poisson expectation."
with(EX$summary_ext, tibble::tibble(
  Lag = c("peak", "1 km", "2 km", "5 km", "10 km", "20 km"),
  `g_inhom` = round(c(peak_g, g_1km, g_2km, g_5km, g_10km, g_20km), 2),
  Note = c(glue("at {round(peak_r_m)} m"), "", "", "", "", "sampling noise at this lag")
)) |> kable(align = "lrl")
```

```{r}
#| label: ext-crosscheck
#| include: false
cc <- EX$correction_cmp
cc_med <- 100 * median(abs(cc$rel_diff), na.rm = TRUE)
```

I cross-checked the extended curve against my @sec-honest-test estimate over the lags
both cover, since both use the translation correction. The median relative difference
is `r sprintf("%.2f%%", cc_med)`, so changing the $r$ grid has not quietly changed
the estimate underneath me.

**So here is my corrected answer to Q3.** Residual clustering begins immediately
above the sensor floor, is strongest at roughly
`r round(EX$summary_ext$peak_r_m)` m, and only decays to within 10% of no excess by
about `r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km. My earlier
statement that the excess was exhausted by 2 km was simply an artefact of not having
looked far enough, and the conclusion I drew from it, that the first-order surface
was a sufficient description above 2 km, was wrong. It is not sufficient at any lag
below roughly 7 km.

# Spatio-temporal analysis {#sec-spacetime}

## Space-time interaction

```{r tbl-knox}
#| label: tbl-knox
#| tbl-cap: "Knox test of space-time interaction across a grid of spatial and temporal thresholds. Each cell counts observed pairs close in both space and time, against the mean under 999 random labellings in which locations and dates are held fixed and only their pairing is permuted. The ratio is observed over expected."
ST$knox_tab |> transmute(
  `Space (m)` = fmt_n(s_m), `Time (days)` = t_days,
  Observed = fmt_n(observed), `Expected` = fmt_n(round(exp_perm)),
  Ratio = round(ratio, 2),
  `p-value` = vapply(p_value, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = ST$nperm)) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrrr")
```

```{r fig-knox}
#| label: fig-knox
#| fig-cap: "Knox ratio of observed to expected close pairs, by spatial and temporal threshold. What I take from it: interaction is strongest in the tightest cell, pairs within a few hundred metres and one day, and decays monotonically as either threshold widens. That shape is the signature of local, short-lived propagation: a cell that burns today makes a neighbouring cell more likely to burn tomorrow, and the effect is largely spent within a few days and a kilometre or two. The decay in the time direction is steeper than in the space direction, which is consistent with fires spreading over contiguous ground within days rather than recurring in the same place weeks apart. Because the null holds both marginals fixed, none of this can be attributed to the seasonal escalation in @fig-daily."
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(ST$knox_tab, aes(factor(s_m), factor(t_days), fill = ratio)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", ratio)), size = 3.1, colour = PAL$ink,
            family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Observed / expected") +
  labs(x = "Spatial threshold (m)", y = "Temporal threshold (days)",
       title = "Interaction is local in space and short in time",
       subtitle = glue("{fmt_n(ST$n_close_pairs)} close pairs, {ST$nperm} random labellings.")) +
  theme_ex01(grid = "none")
```

## Does the signature move between onset and peak?

```{r fig-rr}
#| label: fig-rr
#| fig-cap: "Probability that a burned cell belongs to the peak period rather than the onset period, as a spatially varying surface. Values above the overall peak share indicate areas where fire arrived late; values below indicate areas that burned early. What I take from it: the surface is not flat, so the episode is not a uniform intensification of one fixed footprint. The southern and southeastern peat burned disproportionately early, while the northern and western margins of the active area contribute disproportionately to the peak period. Read together with the weekly trajectory below, this describes an episode that begins in the most degraded peat and expands outward from it. The operational implication I draw is that where fire is early in the season carries information about where it will appear later, which my static seasonal intensity map cannot convey."
#| fig-height: 6.2
rr_df <- im_df(ST$rr, "p")
share_peak <- as.numeric(ST$season_counts["peak"]) / sum(ST$season_counts)
ggplot(rr_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = p)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = PAL$cool, mid = PAL$ground_alt, high = PAL$accent_dk,
                       midpoint = share_peak, name = "P(peak period)",
                       labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "The episode expands rather than intensifies in place",
       subtitle = glue("Split at {format(ST$split_date, '%d %B')}. Midpoint of the scale is the overall peak share, {percent(share_peak, accuracy = 1)}.")) +
  theme_map()
```

```{r fig-traj}
#| label: fig-traj
#| fig-cap: "Weekly mean centre of burned cells with the weekly dispersion about it, and the distance the centre moved each week. What I take from it: the mean centre is a crude summary and I use it only for what it does reliably, which is showing direction and spread over time. Dispersion widens as the season progresses, which confirms the expansion I read off the relative-risk surface. The weekly displacement of the centre is largest in the early weeks, when few cells dominate the mean, and settles to a few kilometres a week once activity is widespread. The caution I would attach is that the mean centre of a strongly non-convex, multi-modal pattern is not a place where anything is happening. It is a summary statistic and I would not put it on an operational map."
#| fig-height: 3.6
tr <- ST$traj |> filter(n > 0)
p_sd <- ggplot(tr, aes(week_start, sd_km)) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 4.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Standard distance (km)", subtitle = "Dispersion of burned cells") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b") + theme_ex01()
p_step <- ggplot(tr |> filter(!is.na(step_km)), aes(week_start, step_km)) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent_dk, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent_dk, size = 1.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weekly shift of mean centre (km)", subtitle = "Movement of the mean centre") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b") + theme_ex01()
p_sd + p_step + plot_annotation(
  title = "The footprint widens as the season progresses", theme = theme_ex01())
```

## Space-time intensity

```{r fig-st}
#| label: fig-st
#| fig-cap: "Space-time intensity at fortnightly reference days, estimated with a fixed spatial kernel and a Gaussian weight in time of five days' standard deviation. Each panel is normalised to its own weights, so panels show where fire was concentrated at that moment rather than how much there was. What I take from it: the sequence makes the expansion explicit. Early July activity is confined to a small southeastern area. Through August the active area extends north and west along the peat belt while retaining the southern core. By mid-September activity covers most of the southern two-thirds of the regency. My estimator assumes separability, meaning the spatial kernel does not change shape over time. That is a simplification: the real footprint is elongating, and a separable estimator can only show that as a change in weights."
#| fig-height: 4.4
st_df <- bind_rows(lapply(ST$st_kde, function(s)
  im_df(s$im) |> mutate(panel = format(s$date, "%d %b"))))
st_df$panel <- factor(st_df$panel, levels = vapply(ST$st_kde,
                                                   function(s) format(s$date, "%d %b"), character(1)))
ggplot(st_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = intensity / max(intensity, na.rm = TRUE))) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.22) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Relative intensity",
                       labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Fire spreads north and west from a southeastern origin") +
  theme_map(base_size = 8)
```

# An areal check: spatial autocorrelation

Everything so far treats the data as a point pattern. Aggregating to areal units
and computing Moran's I looks at the same question through different machinery:
contiguity weights and a permutation test on counts share no assumptions with
$K_{inhom}$ and its envelopes. If the two agree, that is worth more than either
alone.

It needs setting up carefully, because the obvious version repeats the mistake @sec-strawman is built around. Moran's I on raw burned-cell counts will be large and
significant here whatever the fire does. Intensity varies by two orders of
magnitude between the peat belt and the northern interior, so adjacent hexagons in
the south are both high and adjacent hexagons in the north are both low. The counts
are autocorrelated by construction. That is the first-order trend, measured again
in a new coordinate system.

The informative version asks whether autocorrelation survives the trend. Each
hexagon gets an expected count by integrating $\hat{\lambda}$ over it, and the
variable analysed is the Pearson residual
$(\text{observed} - \text{expected}) / \sqrt{\text{expected}}$. That is the areal
analogue of swapping CSR for an inhomogeneous Poisson null.

**Hexagons, not squares.** @sec-isotropy found that a square 375 m lattice imprints
its geometry on short-range structure. A square aggregation grid has the same
defect: four edge neighbours and four corner neighbours sitting at different
distances. A hexagonal tessellation gives six neighbours all equidistant.

```{r tbl-moran}
#| label: tbl-moran
#| tbl-cap: "Global Moran's I on hexagonal aggregations of three sizes, for raw counts and for Pearson residuals after the kernel intensity is removed. Weights are queen contiguity, row-standardised. The expectation under no autocorrelation is close to zero in every row."
LI$global |> transmute(
  `Hex size` = hex_size, Variable = variable, Units = fmt_n(n_units),
  `Mean neighbours` = round(mean_nb, 2),
  `Moran I` = round(moran_I, 3), `z` = round(z, 1),
  `p` = ifelse(p < 1e-12, "< 1e-12", format.pval(p, digits = 2))
) |> kable(align = "llrrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: moran-inline
#| include: false
gg <- LI$global
gr <- function(sz, v) gg$moran_I[gg$hex_size == sz & grepl(v, gg$variable)]
zr <- function(sz, v) gg$z[gg$hex_size == sz & grepl(v, gg$variable)]
cnt <- LI$counts
hh_raw <- cnt$`raw count`[cnt$cluster == "High-High"]
sig_res <- sum(cnt$residual[cnt$cluster != "not significant"])
```

```{r fig-moran}
#| label: fig-moran
#| fig-cap: "Global Moran's I against hexagon size, for raw counts and for residuals. What I take from it: the raw-count line barely moves, because the trend it is measuring exists at every scale. The residual line falls steeply, from 0.42 at 2 km to 0.07 at 5 km. That decay is the point of the figure. It is what the pair correlation function predicts independently, having found the excess concentrated below about 2 km and gone by 7 km. Aggregating into 5 km hexagons absorbs almost all of the structure into the units themselves, so little is left to show up between them."
#| fig-height: 3.2
gm <- LI$global |> mutate(size_km = as.numeric(sub(" km", "", hex_size)),
                          v = ifelse(grepl("raw", variable), "Raw count", "Residual"))
ggplot(gm, aes(size_km, moran_I, colour = v, group = v)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Raw count` = PAL$cool, Residual = PAL$accent), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = LI$sizes / 1000, labels = function(x) paste0(x, " km")) +
  labs(x = "Hexagon size", y = "Global Moran's I",
       title = "Removing the trend removes most of the autocorrelation",
       subtitle = "And what remains decays as the units grow past the interaction scale.") +
  theme_ex01()
```

## What the local statistics say

```{r fig-lisa}
#| label: fig-lisa
#| fig-cap: "Local Moran clusters at 3 km, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted across 1,252 simultaneous tests. Left, raw counts. Right, residuals after the kernel intensity is removed. What I take from it: the left map rediscovers the peat belt and nothing else. Its 105 High-High hexagons are the same southern concentration the intensity surface already shows, arrived at by a different route. The right map is empty. Not one hexagon survives correction, and the smallest adjusted p-value is 0.066. The residual autocorrelation that the global statistic detects is real but diffuse, spread thinly across the map instead of concentrated anywhere a planner could point at."
#| fig-height: 6.4
lis <- bind_rows(
  LI$hex |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(hex_id, cluster = cl_raw, panel = "Raw counts"),
  LI$hex |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(hex_id, cluster = cl_resid, panel = "Residuals after lambda-hat")) |>
  left_join(LI$hex |> select(hex_id), by = "hex_id") |> st_as_sf()
cols <- c("High-High" = PAL$accent_dk, "Low-Low" = PAL$cool,
          "High-Low" = PAL$accent_lt, "Low-High" = "#8FBDC0",
          "not significant" = PAL$ground_alt)
ggplot(lis) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cluster), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "The local statistics find the peat belt, and nothing beyond it") +
  theme_map(base_size = 9)
```

### Reading it against the point-pattern result

**The two methods agree, and that is the main value of doing both.** Removing
$\hat{\lambda}$ cuts global Moran's I from `r round(gr("3 km","raw"), 2)` to
`r round(gr("3 km","Pearson"), 2)` at 3 km. What remains is significant
(z = `r round(zr("3 km","Pearson"), 1)`) and decays steeply as the hexagons grow,
reaching `r round(gr("5 km","Pearson"), 2)` at 5 km. An areal method with
contiguity weights and a point-pattern method with edge-corrected distance
statistics both put residual structure below a few kilometres and nothing much
above it.

**The local statistics add a caution the global ones do not.** On raw counts,
`r hh_raw` hexagons come out High-High, and they are the peat belt. On residuals,
`r sig_res` survive correction. The residual autocorrelation is genuine in
aggregate and too thin to localise.

That matters for how the earlier results should be used. @sec-cluster-size gives a cluster
radius near a kilometre, which is a statement about typical scale. It is not a
claim that particular places have persistently more clustering than the intensity
surface predicts, and this section is the check that would have found such places
if they existed.

**Two caveats.** The modifiable areal unit problem is unavoidable here, which is
why three resolutions are reported instead of one; the raw-count conclusion is
stable across them and the residual magnitude is not. And Benjamini-Hochberg across
1,252 tests is doing real work. Without it, an unadjusted 5% test would be expected
to mark about 60 hexagons by chance alone, which would have made a convincing and
entirely spurious map of residual hotspots.

# Value-added analysis {#sec-valueadded}

So far I have established that fire is clustered, where it concentrates, and over
what distance and time the interaction operates. What I still cannot say is what the
clustering is organised around, or how big a cluster actually is. Both are
answerable, and both are what turn a statistical result into something an agency
could act on, so I went after them.

## What is the clustering organised around? {#sec-covariates}

Peat fire here is human in ignition and made possible by drainage. Two mapped
covariates proxy those mechanisms: distance to the road network for access and
ignition opportunity, distance to mapped canals and waterways for drainage-driven
desiccation.

I took the covariate geometry from a dated Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extract for
Kalimantan rather than a live Overpass query. That was not my first choice. Overpass
refused a bounding box this size repeatedly, and once I had switched I realised the
extract is better anyway: a live query returns different data every time it runs, so
it cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline. The extract gave me
`r fmt_n(CM$n_roads)` road features and `r fmt_n(CM$n_water)` waterway features
within a 15 km buffer of the regency.

I compute distances on that buffered frame and only then crop to the analysis
window. If I had computed them on the clipped window I would have biased every
distance upward for cells near the boundary, because their nearest road is often
outside the regency entirely.

The same reasoning caught a bug in my first land-cover attempt, and it is worth
recording because it fails quietly. `distmap` returns distances on the enclosing
frame of whatever you hand it. Handed the union of the landuse polygons, that frame
is their own bounding box, so the covariate was undefined across 98% of the regency
and `ppm` fitted on the 2% that remained. The AIC values it returned were in the
hundreds against tens of thousands for the other models, which is the only reason I
looked. Evaluating `distfun` over the analysis window fixes it. Nothing in the
report rests on the broken version, but a less absurd set of numbers would have gone
unnoticed.

The `r fmt_n(CM$n_water)` waterway features against `r fmt_n(CM$n_roads)` road
features is itself my first result here, and it is a warning rather than a finding.
An area defined by an abandoned canal network has fewer mapped watercourses than
roads. I come back to what that does to the drainage covariate below.

```{r fig-rho}
#| label: fig-rho
#| fig-cap: "Estimated intensity as a non-parametric function of distance to the nearest road and to the nearest mapped waterway, with 95% confidence bands. The horizontal line is the mean intensity over the window. What I take from it: intensity falls steeply with distance from a road, from well above the window mean within the first kilometre to below it beyond a few kilometres. That is a strong and monotone access effect, consistent with ignition being human. The waterway relationship is weaker and less monotone. This is my more interesting negative result. It does not show drainage is unimportant, it shows OpenStreetMap's waterway layer is a poor proxy for it, because the dense minor canal network of the former Mega Rice Project is largely unmapped. My covariate is measuring mapping effort as much as hydrology, so I read the flat curve as absence of evidence."
#| fig-height: 3.6
rho_to_df <- function(rh, lab) {
  if (is.null(rh)) return(NULL)
  d <- rh
  nm <- names(d)
  tibble(x = d[[1]], rho = d[["rho"]],
         lo = if ("lo" %in% nm) d[["lo"]] else NA_real_,
         hi = if ("hi" %in% nm) d[["hi"]] else NA_real_, panel = lab)
}
rho_df <- bind_rows(
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_road,  "Distance to nearest road"),
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_water, "Distance to nearest mapped waterway"))
mean_int <- P$ppp_cell$n / (P$area_km2 * 1e6)
if (!is.null(rho_df) && nrow(rho_df)) {
  ggplot(rho_df, aes(x / 1000)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = per_1000km2(mean_int) / 1e3 * 1e3,
               colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
                fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km²",
         title = "Access explains a great deal, mapped drainage very little",
         subtitle = "Dashed line, mean intensity over the window.") +
    theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
} else cat("Covariate estimation unavailable; see the limitations.\n")
```

```{r tbl-aic}
#| label: tbl-aic
#| tbl-cap: "Fitted Poisson point-process models compared by AIC. Distances are in kilometres, so coefficients read per kilometre. The log specification was included on the expectation that a steep near-field effect flattening with distance would fit better than a linear term; it does not, and is reported as a failed expectation rather than dropped."
CM$aic_tab |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                        AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC)), `Delta AIC` = fmt_n(round(dAIC))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: aic-inline
#| include: false
dn <- CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "null"]
dr <- dn - CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "road"]
dw <- dn - CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "water"]
dboth_over_road <- CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "road"]
```

```{r tbl-aic2}
#| label: tbl-aic2
#| tbl-cap: "Models compared by AIC once land cover is included. `access` is distance to road and to mapped waterway; `cover` is distance to mapped forest and to plantation or farmland. Both have three parameters, so they are directly comparable."
BC$aic2 |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                     AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC)), `Delta AIC` = fmt_n(round(dAIC))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: aic2-inline
#| include: false
g <- function(m) BC$aic2$dAIC[BC$aic2$model == m]
dn2 <- g("null"); d_road <- dn2 - g("road"); d_cover <- dn2 - g("cover")
d_access <- dn2 - g("access")
cf <- as.data.frame(BC$best_coef2)
co <- function(n) cf[n, "Estimate"]; zz <- function(n) cf[n, "Zval"]
sh <- BC$cover_share
```

Adding land cover changed which mechanism looks dominant, and the earlier version of
this section had it wrong. Checking the support behind each covariate then corrected
me a second time, in the other direction.

```{r tbl-coversplit}
#| label: tbl-coversplit
#| tbl-cap: "Each covariate fitted on its own, so the explanatory power can be attributed rather than shared. Gain is the AIC improvement over an intercept-only model. The single-covariate models all use two parameters and are directly comparable."
CS$aic |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                    `Gain over null` = fmt_n(round(gain_over_null)),
                    AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC))) |> kable(align = "lrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: cs-inline
#| include: false
gn <- function(m) CS$aic$gain_over_null[CS$aic$model == m]
sup <- CS$support
cf <- as.data.frame(BC$best_coef2)
co <- function(n) cf[n, "Estimate"]; zz <- function(n) cf[n, "Zval"]
sh <- BC$cover_share
```

**Proximity to plantation and farmland is the covariate that matters.** On its own
it recovers `r fmt_n(round(gn("plantation")))` of the
`r fmt_n(round(gn("all")))` AIC units the full model gains over an intercept-only
model, which is about
`r percent(gn("plantation")/gn("all"), accuracy = 1)` of the total from a single
term. Distance to road recovers `r fmt_n(round(gn("road")))` and distance to forest
`r fmt_n(round(gn("forest")))`, both on the same two parameters.

My earlier claim that access did nearly all the work was an artefact of a thin
covariate set. With only roads and waterways in the model, distance to road was the
best available proxy for something it was not measuring.

**The forest term is much weaker than I first reported, and I should not have read
it as a mechanism.** Adding forest on top of plantation buys only
`r fmt_n(round(gn("cover_both") - gn("plantation")))` further AIC units, and forest
alone explains slightly less than roads alone. The reason is visible in the support
behind it. The median burned cell sits
`r round(sup$median_km[sup$feature == "forest"], 1)` km from the nearest mapped
forest polygon and
`r percent(sup$share_beyond_20km[sup$feature == "forest"], accuracy = 1)` of cells
are beyond 20 km, so the covariate is describing a near-regional gradient across an
86 km wide window. Plantation sits at a median of
`r round(sup$median_km[sup$feature == "plantation"], 1)` km, which is a local
relationship.

```{r tbl-coef2}
#| label: tbl-coef2
#| tbl-cap: "Coefficients of the full model, on the log-intensity scale, per kilometre. A negative coefficient means intensity falls with distance from that feature. The forest coefficient is positive and precisely estimated, but see the caution below: a linear term summarises a relationship that the non-parametric curve shows is not monotone."
tibble::tibble(
  Covariate = c("Distance to road", "Distance to waterway",
                "Distance to forest", "Distance to plantation or farmland"),
  Estimate = round(cf[c("Droad_km","Dwater_km","Dforest_km","Dplantation_km"), "Estimate"], 4),
  `Std. error` = round(cf[c("Droad_km","Dwater_km","Dforest_km","Dplantation_km"), "S.E."], 4),
  `z` = round(cf[c("Droad_km","Dwater_km","Dforest_km","Dplantation_km"), "Zval"], 1)
) |> kable(align = "lrrr")
```

**What the signs support, and what they do not.** Intensity rises steeply as you
approach plantation and farmland (coefficient `r round(co("Dplantation_km"), 4)`,
z = `r round(zz("Dplantation_km"), 1)`). That relationship is local, monotone and
carries most of the model, and for peat fire used in land clearing it is the
expected pattern.

The forest coefficient is positive and has a large z, but a large z on a
misspecified functional form is not evidence of a mechanism. The rhohat curve below
is not monotone: intensity is moderate near mapped forest, higher at 20 to 25 km,
low at 40 km and high again beyond. A single linear term across that range is a
summary, not a description. What I can say is that mapped forest and fire are
largely in different parts of the regency. What I cannot say is that proximity to
forest suppresses fire.

**The OSM caveat applies to both, with different force.** Mapped forest covers
`r percent(sh$share_of_window[sh$group == "forest"], accuracy = 0.1)` of the window
and plantation or farmland
`r percent(sh$share_of_window[sh$group == "plantation"], accuracy = 0.1)`, from a
few dozen polygons apiece. For plantation the effect is local and steep enough that
mapping effort is an unlikely explanation. For forest, where the covariate varies
over tens of kilometres, I cannot separate the two.

**None of this is causal.** Roads, farmland and forest edges are jointly determined
by where people have cleared and worked the land. The model orders covariates by
explanatory power. It does not say what would happen if any of them changed.

```{r fig-rho2}
#| label: fig-rho2
#| fig-cap: "Intensity as a non-parametric function of distance to mapped forest and to plantation or farmland, with 95% bands. What I take from it: the two panels are not equally trustworthy and the figure is the reason I stopped treating them as a pair. Plantation falls steeply over the first few kilometres and is the strongest covariate relationship in the report; the median burned cell is 4 km from mapped plantation, so the informative part of that curve is where the data is. Forest is a different matter. The curve is not monotone, rising to 20 to 25 km, dropping near 40 and rising again, and the median cell sits 20 km out with half beyond that. The positive linear coefficient in the model is a summary of that shape, not a description of it."
#| fig-height: 3.6
rc <- bind_rows(lapply(names(BC$rho_cover), function(nm) {
  d <- BC$rho_cover[[nm]]; names(d)[1] <- "x"
  d |> transmute(x, rho, lo, hi,
                 panel = ifelse(nm == "forest", "Distance to mapped forest",
                                "Distance to plantation or farmland"))
}))
ggplot(rc, aes(x / 1000)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
              fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km\u00b2",
       title = "One curve is local and steep, the other is neither") +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

### What the covariates still fail to explain

```{r fig-resk}
#| label: fig-resk
#| fig-cap: "Residual K function for the best-fitting Poisson model, which is the full model with road, water, forest and plantation distances. If the fitted trend explained the pattern this curve would sit on zero. What I take from it: it does not. A large positive residual remains at short lags, so the covariates account for a great deal of the first-order variation and none of the local interaction. Knowing how far a place is from cleared land tells me whether it is likely to burn. It does not tell me that burning spreads. A Poisson model cannot represent contagion by construction, which is what motivates the cluster process fitted next."
#| fig-height: 3.4
rk <- RK$res_K
ycol <- if ("bres" %in% names(rk)) "bres" else names(rk)[2]
ggplot(rk, aes(r, .data[[ycol]])) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = "Residual K",
       title = "The covariates explain location, not contagion",
       subtitle = glue("Model: {RK$formula}")) +
  theme_ex01()
```

## How large is a cluster? {#sec-cluster-size}

A significance test says clustering exists. A fitted cluster process says how big it
is, which is the form a planner can use. Getting that number right meant discarding
my first answer.

The first fit had no trend term. It returned a cluster standard deviation of
`r fmt_n(round(TH$kppm_hom$sigma_m))` m, about
`r round(TH$kppm_hom$mu_per_cluster)` events per cluster, and an implied
`r round(TH$kppm_hom$kappa_per_km2 * P$area_km2)` parent locations across the whole
regency. Twenty-three clusters of 440 events each is not a cluster scale. It is the
southern peat belt re-described as a handful of enormous clusters, which is the only
way a model without a trend term can represent large-scale intensity variation.
Trend and interaction are not separately identifiable unless you make them so. Taken
at face value the number would have given a confident and completely wrong
operational radius.

The fix is to remove the trend before estimating the cluster parameters. My
inhomogeneous pair correlation function already does exactly that, because it divides
out $\hat{\lambda}(u)$. So I fitted the Thomas pair correlation function

$$g(r) \;=\; 1 + \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\sigma^{2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right)$$

directly to $g_{inhom}$ by minimum contrast, minimising
$\sum_r \left(\hat{g}(r)^{q} - g_\theta(r)^{q}\right)^{2}$ with $q = 1/4$ over
$r \in [`r TH$RMIN`, `r fmt_n(TH$RMAX)`]$ m. I set the lower limit to exclude lags
governed by the 375 m sensor floor rather than by the cluster process. I wrote the
fit out explicitly in `R/07_cluster_scale.R` rather than calling a packaged routine,
because the objective function and the excluded range are the substance of the
estimate and I wanted them visible.

```{r tbl-thomas}
#| label: tbl-thomas
#| tbl-cap: "Thomas cluster process fitted by minimum contrast, with and without the first-order trend removed. sigma is the standard deviation of offspring displacement from the cluster centre and r95 the radius containing about 95% of a cluster's events. The contrast between the two rows is the finding: leaving the trend in the model inflates the estimated cluster scale by a factor of two, and the implied cluster sizes become absurd."
TH$thomas_tab |> transmute(
  Specification = spec,
  `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
  `r95 (m)` = round(r95_m),
  `Parents in regency` = round(n_parents_implied),
  `Events per cluster` = round(mu_per_cluster)) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: thomas-inline
#| include: false
tp <- TH$thomas_tab |> filter(key == "trend_removed")
r95 <- round(tp$r95_m); sig_t <- round(tp$sigma_m); mu_t <- round(tp$mu_per_cluster)
```

```{r fig-thomas}
#| label: fig-thomas
#| fig-cap: "Observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function with the two fitted Thomas models, log scale, over the range used for fitting. The shaded band marks lags below 200 m, excluded from the fit because they are governed by the sensor's pixel size. What I take from it: the trend-removed fit tracks the observed curve closely from the peak outward, which is the range that matters for an operational radius. The fit that retains the trend is too flat and too wide, because its cluster component is doing work that belongs to the intensity surface. Neither fit captures the observed curve beyond about 4 km, where the observed g_inhom decays more slowly than a single Gaussian cluster kernel allows. That is a real limitation of my model: the pattern has structure at more than one scale, and a one-scale model cannot represent it."
#| fig-height: 3.6
gobs <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, r <= TH$RMAX, is.finite(trans))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = TH$RMIN, ymin = 1, ymax = max(gobs$trans) * 1.05,
           fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = gobs, aes(r, trans), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = TH$curves, aes(r, g, linetype = spec), colour = PAL$cool,
            linewidth = 0.55) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(2, 1), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "Removing the trend halves the estimated cluster scale",
       subtitle = "Orange, observed inhomogeneous pcf. Blue, fitted Thomas models. Shaded, lags excluded from the fit.") +
  theme_ex01()
```

My trend-removed fit gives a cluster standard deviation of `r fmt_n(sig_t)` m, so
about 95% of a cluster's events fall within roughly `r fmt_n(r95)` m of its centre,
with `r mu_t` events per cluster and about `r round(tp$n_parents_implied)` cluster
centres across the regency.

### How precise is that number

Minimum contrast gives no standard error, so the estimate above was unqualified
until I bootstrapped it. My first attempt resampled points with replacement. That is
not a valid bootstrap for a point process: it destroys the dependence being
estimated and creates coincident points, which distorts the pair correlation
function at exactly the short lags the fit uses. The symptom was unmistakable. The
interval excluded the point estimate entirely, and in the wrong direction.

The interval below comes from a parametric bootstrap. I simulate from the fitted
inhomogeneous Thomas process, re-estimate $\hat{\lambda}$ on each simulation,
recompute $g_{inhom}$, and refit by the same minimum contrast.

```{r tbl-boot}
#| label: tbl-boot
#| tbl-cap: "Two bootstrap intervals on the cluster standard deviation. The non-parametric row is shown because it is wrong in an instructive way: an interval that excludes its own point estimate is a sign the resampling scheme does not respect the process."
BC$boot_compare |> transmute(
  Method = method,
  `sigma point (m)` = round(point_sigma_m),
  `median (m)` = round(median_m),
  `95% interval (m)` = glue("{round(lo95_m)} to {round(hi95_m)}"),
  `r95 interval (m)` = glue("{round(r95_lo_m)} to {round(r95_hi_m)}")
) |> kable(align = "lrrll")
```

```{r}
#| label: boot-inline
#| include: false
pb <- BC$boot_compare |> filter(key == "par")
```

The parametric interval puts the cluster standard deviation between
`r fmt_n(round(pb$lo95_m))` and `r fmt_n(round(pb$hi95_m))` m, and the radius
holding 95% of a cluster between `r round(pb$r95_lo_m/1000, 2)` and
`r round(pb$r95_hi_m/1000, 2)` km. The refits sit a little below the point estimate,
a known downward bias of minimum contrast under resimulation, so the point estimate
lies just above its own interval. A cluster scale of about a kilometre, with roughly
2.2 to 2.5 km holding the bulk of one, is the summary I would defend. The
kilometre-scale conclusion does not turn on which end of that range is right. That is
consistent with my pair correlation function, which peaks at
`r round(EX$summary_ext$peak_r_m)` m, and I got there by a different route: minimum
contrast fitting of a mechanistic model rather than envelope testing.

Two estimates agreeing is stronger than either alone, but the agreement is only
partial and I should say where it breaks. My fitted model has a single scale, and
the figure below shows the observed curve decaying more slowly beyond about 4 km
than a single Gaussian kernel allows. So the Thomas process describes the dominant
local structure well and the longer tail of dependence out to roughly
`r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km not at all. A multi-scale
cluster process, or a log-Gaussian Cox process with a flexible covariance, would be
the natural next model. Fitting one is beyond what I can do in this exercise, but it
is the first thing I would try next.

## Where is the single most unusual concentration?

This is the most directly practical question I ask anywhere in the report. Not
whether clustering exists, but where the single most unusual concentration sits and
whether it is more extreme than chance would produce.

```{r tbl-scan}
#| label: tbl-scan
#| tbl-cap: "Spatial scan statistic, Poisson model, circular windows of 2, 5 and 10 km radius, 99 Monte Carlo simulations. The location is the maximum of the likelihood-ratio surface."
sc <- CM$scan_res
lrts <- attr(sc, "obsLRTS")
w  <- which(lrts$v == max(lrts$v, na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
mx <- c(x = lrts$xcol[w[2]], y = lrts$yrow[w[1]])
ll <- st_coordinates(st_transform(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(mx["x"], mx["y"])), crs = STUDY_CRS), 4326))
tibble::tibble(
  `Max likelihood-ratio statistic` = round(as.numeric(sc$statistic), 1),
  `p-value` = fmt_p(sc$p.value, 99),
  `Radii tested (km)` = paste(attr(sc, "r") / 1000, collapse = ", "),
  `Most likely cluster centre` = sprintf("%.3f E, %.3f S", ll[1], abs(ll[2]))
) |> kable(align = "rrll")
```

```{r fig-scan}
#| label: fig-scan
#| fig-cap: "Likelihood-ratio surface from the spatial scan statistic, with the maximum marked. What I take from it: the surface is not a second intensity map. It measures, at each location, how much better a model with an elevated rate inside a circle fits than a model with a constant rate, so it answers where I would look first rather than where fire is densest. The maximum sits in the southern peat belt, consistent with the kernel intensity estimate, and the statistic is significant at the Monte Carlo floor. What this adds over my intensity map is that it is explicitly comparative. The broad plateau shows several locations are nearly as unusual as the maximum, so I would over-read it if I treated the single peak as uniquely important."
#| fig-height: 6.2
ls_df <- im_df(lrts, "lrts")
ggplot(ls_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = lrts)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  annotate("point", x = mx["x"], y = mx["y"], shape = 21, size = 3.4,
           colour = PAL$ink, fill = NA, stroke = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = mx["x"] + 4000, y = mx["y"], label = "maximum",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink, family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Likelihood ratio statistic",
                       labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "Where an agency would look first",
       subtitle = glue("Scan statistic surface, circles of {paste(attr(sc,'r')/1000, collapse=', ')} km.")) +
  theme_map()
```

# Was 2026 unusual? {#sec-multiyear}

An earlier draft said the 87-day window made it impossible to judge whether 2026
was a severe season, and blamed the FIRMS API's 90-day retention. The retention is
real. The inference was not.

The standard-processing product returns nothing for 2026 because near-real-time
granules are replaced by standard science quality only after about five months. For
earlier years the same REST endpoint serves the archive normally. I had tested 2026,
seen zeros, and generalised from one year. A single query against 2019 would have
shown me otherwise.

The multi-year record was reachable from the same key throughout. This section uses
the identical 1 July to 25 September window for every year from
`r min(MY$years_pulled)` to `r max(MY$years_pulled)`.

## Two rules for comparability

**S-NPP only, every year including 2026.** NOAA-20 joins the record in 2018, so
counting two platforms in recent years against one platform in earlier years would
produce a step change in detection capability indistinguishable from a change in
fire. The 2026 figure in this section is therefore *smaller* than the headline
figure elsewhere in the report, which uses both platforms.

**The identical calendar window every year**, so window length cannot be confused
with fire intensity.

One caveat I cannot remove: 2026 is the near-real-time product and every earlier
year is the reprocessed standard product. They differ slightly, and I cannot
quantify by how much, because the retention windows of the two products do not
overlap anywhere in the record. The direction of the likely bias is that
near-real-time retains some detections that reprocessing removes, so the 2026
figure should be read as, if anything, a little generous.

```{r tbl-multiyear}
#| label: tbl-multiyear
#| tbl-cap: "Burned 375 m cells in Pulang Pisau over the identical 1 July to 25 September window, every year of the VIIRS S-NPP record. Rank is over all 14 years."
MY$annual |> transmute(
  Year = year,
  Detections = fmt_n(detections),
  `Burned cells` = fmt_n(cells),
  Rank = rank_cells,
  `vs median` = ifelse(year == 2026, sprintf("%.0fx", vs_median), "")
) |> kable(align = "rrrrr")
```

```{r fig-multiyear}
#| label: fig-multiyear
#| fig-cap: "Burned cells in the same 87-day window, 2013 to 2026, log scale. Reading: this is the figure I could not draw before, and it reframes the whole report. 2026 is not a representative season. It ranks second of fourteen years, roughly fifty times the median, behind only the 2015 El Nino fires and ahead of 2019. The record is also violently bimodal rather than continuous: drought years produce thousands of burned cells and wet years produce single or double digits, with almost nothing in between. That matters for planning, because a capability sized to the median would be overwhelmed in a year like this one, and a capability sized to 2026 would idle for years at a time."
#| fig-height: 3.8
ay <- MY$annual |> mutate(is26 = year == 2026)
ggplot(ay, aes(factor(year), pmax(cells, 1), fill = is26)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median(ay$cells[ay$year != 2026]),
             colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = median(ay$cells[ay$year != 2026]) * 1.5,
           label = "2013-2025 median", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = PAL$accent_lt, `TRUE` = PAL$accent_dk),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Burned cells, log scale",
       title = "2026 is the second-worst season in the VIIRS record here",
       subtitle = glue("Same 1 July to 25 September window every year. S-NPP only, for comparability.")) +
  theme_ex01()
```

```{r}
#| label: my-inline
#| include: false
a26 <- MY$annual |> filter(year == 2026)
hist_med <- median(MY$annual$cells[MY$annual$year != 2026])
worst <- MY$annual |> filter(year != 2026) |> slice_max(cells, n = 1)
```

2026 recorded `r fmt_n(a26$cells)` burned cells in the window, against a
2013 to 2025 median of `r fmt_n(round(hist_med))`. That is
**`r round(a26$vs_median)` times the median** and ranks
**`r a26$rank_cells` of `r nrow(MY$annual)`**, behind only
`r worst$year` (`r fmt_n(worst$cells)` cells).

The gap is so large that the near-real-time versus standard-product caveat cannot
explain it. Reprocessing shifts detection counts by a few percent, not by a factor
of fifty.

There is one thing this understates rather than overstates. My window closes on
25 September because that was the last complete day before I pulled the data, and
@sec-normal-year shows October can be the peak month: in 2023 it carried more burned
cell-days than September did. Every year in the comparison is truncated at the same
point, so the ranking is fair, but the 2026 figure is a season in progress. On the
2023 pattern it could still grow substantially.

## What a normal year looks like {#sec-normal-year}

```{r fig-seasonal}
#| label: fig-seasonal
#| fig-cap: "Monthly burned cell-days across two complete calendar years, log scale, showing the seasonal cycle the 87-day window cannot contain. What I take from it: fire here is not merely seasonal, it is close to switch-like, with wet-season months at or near zero and a dry-season peak orders of magnitude above. But it also corrects an assumption I had been carrying. My window closes on 25 September, and in 2023 the peak month was October, which alone carried more burned cell-days than September. July to September captured only 39% of the 2023 fire year against 67% of 2024. So my window is not the whole fire season, it is the first two thirds of it, and the 2026 figures should be read as a season still in progress rather than a completed total."
#| fig-height: 3.6
sm <- MY$seasonal |> mutate(month_lab = month.abb[month])
sm$month_lab <- factor(sm$month_lab, levels = month.abb)
ggplot(sm, aes(month_lab, pmax(cell_days, 0.5), fill = factor(year))) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.78), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(PAL$accent_lt, PAL$accent_dk), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Burned cell-days, log scale",
       title = "The fire year is close to switch-like",
       subtitle = "Complete calendar years from the standard-processing archive.") +
  theme_ex01()
```

```{r tbl-amplitude}
#| label: tbl-amplitude
#| tbl-cap: "Seasonal concentration in two complete years. The July to September share is the fraction of the year's burned cell-days that fall inside the window this report analyses."
MY$amplitude |> transmute(
  Year = year,
  `Annual burned cell-days` = fmt_n(annual_total),
  `Jul to Sep` = fmt_n(in_window_JulSep),
  `Share in window` = percent(share_JulSep, accuracy = 1),
  `Peak month` = month.abb[peak_month]
) |> kable(align = "rrrrr")
```

## What this does to the rest of the report

No second-order result is overturned. The clustering scale, the Knox interaction
and the covariate relationships are estimated within 2026 and stand on their own.

The interpretation of all of them changes. I thought I was describing the spatial
structure of a dry season. I was describing a severe one, second worst in fourteen
years. A cluster scale near a kilometre and a containment window of days are
properties of extreme conditions. Whether they survive in a median year, when the
regency records a few dozen burned cells instead of eight thousand, this analysis
cannot say. There may be too few events in a median year to estimate them at all.
